howto: Every formula below is the one implemented in the open-source code, with the module named in the margin of each section. Where the code departs from textbook practice, or where a simplification is in force, it is stated as a known limitation rather than hidden. The Methodology tab of the application exports, for each product, an Excel workbook that rebuilds the default trade with live formulas from the user’s own market data next to the engine’s value; those workbooks are the executable companion to this text.
history: 1.46 (23 November 2026). The XVA workbooks of the currency side are a ticket’s own run; no figure of a ticket changes. The forward books (xva\_fx, xva\_crypto) take the forward the ticket’s route reads from the account’s market, run eighteen months, where a ticket’s own grid is monthly, and step each month at the surface’s own vol. A European option on a currency pair and on a digital asset has an XVA workbook (xva\_fx\_option, xva\_crypto\_option), in the ticket’s flat-vol mode. §9 has a replication paragraph for each and states one reading of the option’s run that the book showed; §19 says which mode and which styles are not rebuilt.

1.45 (23 November 2026). More of what a ticket shows can be rebuilt in a spreadsheet; no figure of a ticket changes. A floor and a collar have workbooks of their own, for the price (§6) and for the XVA run (§9); a swaption has an XVA workbook (§9); the forward workbook of a currency pair is carried from the pair’s spot date, as the ticket is (§12). §19 has a table of which instrument has which workbook, and which has none.

1.44 (19 November 2026). The signed record of an option on a rate states the option (§17, record schema v3). No price, risk or XVA figure of a ticket changes. A premium is booked only where the desk enters one (§6). The cap’s XVA workbook was opened in Excel by the project’s owner: every check passed (§9). Until this version a swaption’s record was the swap it delivers: no buyer or seller, no expiry, no premium; a bought and a sold swaption were the same bytes, and the sold one named the wrong payer of each leg. A cap’s, a floor’s and a collar’s record held no premium. The counterparty’s own booking, made from a countersigned record, now holds the opposite side of the option.

1.43 (19 November 2026). A cap, a floor and a collar have XVA (§9, §15). Until this version a ticket’s run refused the three and a netting set’s left them out. Each period of the option is valued on every path by Black’s formula on what one unit grows to over the period, at the variance the paths’ own model gives that growth: on the risk-neutral paths exact but for the payment lag, a martingale when discounted along them, and with no step when a period fixes. The same formula now values a cap or a floor on a swap’s leg, which was valued as a caplet on a rate fixed at its period’s start at the market’s volatility: every such leg’s exposure changes. What a period pays is in the cash a margined run sets against the margin period’s move. On the stack’s market, valued 19 November 2026, uncollateralised at 5,000 paths, seeds 42, 7 and 11, a bought five-year 4.5% cap on ten million: CVA −2,157 to −2,129, FCA about −1,396, no DVA or FBA (a bought cap is never owed by us), KVA −10,917. The model’s variance is not the ticket’s volatility: through the ticket’s formula it is 71.0bp where the ticket prices at 81.5bp, so the paths start about a fifth below the ticket’s price for this cap; both are printed on the tab. A workbook, xva\_cap, rebuilds the run in cells. The table of comparisons in §18 is printed again from the suite: 84 lines where it had 70, the comparisons added since it was last printed among them.

1.42 (19 November 2026). A cap, a floor and a collar are priced as they are booked (§6); the value of every such ticket changes, and so does the value of a booked one. The ticket priced a schedule of its own (from two calendar days after the valuation date, weekend or not, ACT/360 whatever its day count, the dates typed on it unread), and a booked option fell to the desk’s default volatility of 85bp whenever its remaining life was not a quoted maturity of the surface, which is on all but a few days of its life. The ticket now prices the leg it books, and the surface is read between its maturities. On the market the tests run on (the local stack’s seed of 2 November 2026), valued 19 November 2026, a five-year 4.5% cap on ten million read 97,183 on its ticket and 105,015 once booked; both are now 97,322. A booked cap, floor or collar, and a cap or a floor on a swap’s leg, steps in value on the day of the change; a cap’s volatility has no step in the P&L explain (§11), so that day’s step is in its residual. A cap’s or a floor’s strike left blank is at the money; the side signs every figure, a swaption’s too (§5.3). The three routes take 1, 2, 4 or 12 periods a year, the frequencies a leg is scheduled at. The cap workbook is the ticket’s own trade.

1.41 (18 November 2026). The replication of a rates ticket’s XVA (§9); no figure changes. The workbook rebuilt a generic swap whose legs settle every month on today’s discounting, the run of before version 1.34; it now rebuilds the ticket’s own run, cell by cell.

1.40 (18 November 2026). The volatility of a swaption on a ticket (§5.3); the value of every swaption ticket on which no volatility is typed changes. An untouched ticket priced at 86.5bp whatever its expiry, its tenor or the day’s surface; it now reads the desk’s at-the-money swaption grid at the nearest point, the rule a booked option was already revalued on, and says which point and which day. At the money the price is proportional to the volatility, so the change is the ratio of the two: on the reference market of the tests, 94.9bp at one year into five, +9.7%. A currency with no surface takes the desk default of 85bp, −1.7%. A typed volatility is unchanged.

1.39 (18 November 2026). The expiry of a swaption on a ticket (§5.2); a European swaption’s ticket value changes where its tenor is not a whole number of 365-day years, and the swap it delivers ends on the right day. A tenor (now one month to ten years) is that many calendar months from the valuation date, or the expiry is a date typed in. The option’s time is the days to that date over 365, the convention the booked option was already revalued on; a ticket priced a tenor at its nominal fraction of a year, so a three-month option struck on 18 November 2026 ran 0.25 where the calendar gives 92/365, a price 0.41% lower at the money. The swap delivered ended a day short whenever a leap day fell inside it. Nothing changes for a booked trade’s dates.

1.38 (18 November 2026). The hosted demo’s interest-rate curves are synthetic (§14); every rates figure of the demo changes with them. Until now each curve was built from a published overnight fixing and government yields with a stated spread. The firm holds no licence for any benchmark, and some need one to build a curve from or to value with, so the demo no longer reads any: one stated generator makes every curve, every past day’s curve and every overnight fixing. A self-hosted desk connects its own market data and none of this applies to it.

1.37 (17 November 2026). Wording only; no figure changes. The licensed margin methodology the engine does not compute is named once, in §9, where the initial margin is described; elsewhere the margin is called what it is, the desk’s amount or the engine’s own estimate.

1.36 (17 November 2026). Two corrections found by putting one trade through every XVA run (§10). The counterparty run’s capital charge is on each trade’s own asset class: it took the interest-rate add-on on the set’s gross notional whatever the set held, so the incremental KVA of a currency forward was a seventeenth of its ticket’s and a digital-asset forward’s was zero. And under a margin agreement a payment takes its collateral with it: a package leg that settled was taken out of the value and not out of the collateral, which left the whole payment owed for half a step (on a margined calendar spread whose near leg pays 1.7 million, a DVA of 49 where it is 0.9).

1.35 (17 November 2026). The exposure is discounted on its own path (§10); CVA, DVA, FCA and FBA of every rates ticket and of every counterparty run change, by about 2% on a five-year swap. Each charge is, by definition, on E[D(t)V±(t)]; the engine had taken P(0,t)E[V±(t)], which leaves out that a swap’s exposure and its discount factor move together. Found by running one swap through ORE (the Open Source Risk Engine) and this engine like for like, and confirmed against a strip of QuantLib swaptions: the first outside figures for an adjustment.

1.34 (17 November 2026). A rates ticket’s XVA is of the trade itself (§9); every rates ticket’s exposure and adjustments change. Until now the ticket ran a generic swap of its notional, coupon and original tenor whose two legs settle every month: a yearly swap’s last year of exposure, a stored trade’s remaining life and a swaption (whose terms the run did not read: its figures were a swap’s) were not in it. The paths now value the trade’s own legs on their own dates, by the valuation of §15, and a ticket and a netting set of that trade alone are one calculation (within 0.2%, tested). A cap, floor or collar has no XVA until it is valued on the paths, and the tab says so.

1.33 (17 November 2026). No formula changed. The validation paragraph and the cap’s time convention are worded by their evidence: the QuantLib reference suite of §18, which runs on every commit, and the market’s convention.

1.32 (17 November 2026). A correction in counterparty credit (§15); every swap’s exposure there changes, and with it the report’s PFE, EPE and CVA, the incremental charge and the XVA P&L that reads them. Between coupon dates a swap’s floating leg was valued as if it reset on the valuation date, leaving out the interest accrued since its period began: a swap whose two legs pay on the same dates showed the fixed coupon building up with nothing against it, up to a whole coupon before each payment. Each floating period is now valued on its own dates and carries its accrued interest, a payment some days after the period’s end included. Found by putting one trade through every XVA run; the ticket’s stand-alone XVA figures were not affected, the incremental charge beneath them was.

1.31 (17 November 2026). First to default (§10); CVA and DVA of every run change. CVA counts the counterparty’s default only while the desk has not defaulted before it, and DVA the desk’s own only while the counterparty has not: each step’s default probability is weighted by the other party’s survival at the middle of the step, and on a path where a party’s default is tied to the asset, by its survival on that path. On the pinned five-year swap with no margin CVA is 2.5% smaller and DVA 3.6%. DVA and FBA now carry one weight and together credit the funding spread once (they stood 4.8 to 4.9% above it). The two figures without the weight are in every answer.

1.30 (17 November 2026). The funding adjustment (§10); FCA, FBA and the totals that carry them change. The benefit is charged on the funding basis, the funding spread less the desk’s own credit spread, where it was a fixed 55% of the funding spread: DVA already credits the desk with its own credit spread on what it owes, and a benefit at the whole funding spread counted that part twice. Cost and benefit run only while both parties are alive: each step is weighted by the chance that neither has defaulted. A spread curve quoted by tenor is read as a term spread in the funding adjustment as it is in the credit triangle, so each step is charged the forward spread: FCA and MVA on a rising funding curve are higher than before, and a flat spread is unchanged. On the pinned five-year swap with no margin FCA moves from −1,423 to −1,319 and FBA from 1,532 to 623. No adjustment’s sign is set at the end of the run: each is reported as it was accumulated. A swap in a currency other than the dollar is simulated on volatility calibrated to dollar swaptions, and its XVA tab now says so (§9).

1.29 (16 November 2026). A single currency forward and a European option under a scenario are priced by the engine, as every other style already was (§13): the forward by the pricer’s own line, the European on the forward and the discount factor themselves, so the unshocked figure is the ticket’s own to the last digit; the browser’s closed form stands in only while the engine’s answer is on its way. A package’s figures are still the closed form over its legs.

1.28 (16 November 2026). One name for a digital asset’s basis sensitivity wherever it is read (§12, §13): the Excel replications of the digital-asset forward and option carry CRYBASIS01 with the screens’ sign (the negative of the asset-rate bump), where they had kept the earlier name FUND01 and its sign. No figure on any screen changes; the workbook’s row changes its name and its sign.

1.27 (16 November 2026). A collar’s legs are priced on the ticket’s own payment periods (§6): its pricing route had priced both legs quarterly whatever the ticket’s frequency. A quarterly collar is unchanged; a collar at another frequency is now the cap less the floor at that frequency. Valued 2 November 2026 on a flat curve (a continuously compounded zero rate of 3.5%) at a normal volatility of 85bp, a five-year 4.5%/2.5% collar on ten million is −5,943 quarterly, −3,161 semi-annual, +2,365 annual and −7,799 monthly; before, the ticket read −5,943 at every frequency.

1.26 (16 November 2026). The scenario of an option of any style (§13): an American, digital, barrier, double-barrier or touch option on a currency pair or a digital asset is priced by the engine at the scenario’s spot, forward, discount factor and volatility, and a spot at or beyond a barrier is valued as touched, the limit of the pricer there. A package’s option legs read a shock of the surface’s tenors each at its own expiry. A Bermudan swaption’s volatility shock moves the Hull–White σ the tree is built on (§6, Scenario). No price of a ticket changes.

1.25 (15 November 2026). The scenario tab of a rates ticket (§6): the engine on a moved market, a curve shocked by its quotes and a volatility by its points, the trade held where it was on the smile while the curve moves; no price changes. A currency or digital-asset option’s volatility shocked tenor by tenor (§13).

1.23 (15 November 2026). Names and signs of the valuation adjustments (§10); no figure changes. The funding cost is FCA and the funding benefit FBA; FVA is the two together. Until this version the cost alone was called FVA. Every adjustment is written signed as its effect on our value, a cost negative and a benefit positive, which is how the engine has always returned them; the formulas had been written as magnitudes. The adjustments are valuation and are filed as such, apart from counterparty risk, which is exposure against limits.

1.22 (15 November 2026). The ladder at each quoted tenor (§14): beside the four buckets, every quote of a curve is moved on its own and the trade repriced, which is the risk at the instrument one would hedge with. A bucket’s figure is unchanged; a point is the slope at its quote, so a trade’s points add up to its bucket to within the bucket’s own convexity. A cap’s volatility is read as a continuous function of the strike’s distance from the money (§6): the prices of caps, floors and collars move by a little, and their rate risk no longer depends on the size of the move. Compared with QuantLib at single quotes (§18).

1.21 (14 November 2026). A currency non-deliverable forward’s fixing (§12): the rate fixed is the spot rate for delivery on the fixing date’s spot date, so an NDF fixed two business days before it settles is worth what the deliverable forward is, in the quote currency (Nb​(X−K)) or the base currency (Nb​(X−K)/X), and one that fixes earlier is read at that earlier delivery date and carried to the settlement date in the currency it is paid in; from the fixing date the trade is that one amount, on the fixing a desk enters for the source its record names or, until then, on the stored spot and marked provisional. Until this version an NDF never became a fixed amount, and its record named neither a real fixing date nor the currency it settled in.

1.20 (12 November 2026). A backtest of the level a digital asset’s exposure paths simulate, against five years of public daily closes (§9.3): against the bands their own simulated histories give, the regimes are outside in 1 cell of 60 and one volatility in 17; and one MVA figure derived apart from the engine. No figure the engine computes changes.

1.19 (12 November 2026). A barrier is watched between the exposure grid’s dates as well as on them, by the Brownian bridge’s crossing probability, and the desk’s record that a barrier was touched is read by the settlement and the valuation (§13).

1.18 (12 November 2026). Currency and digital-asset tickets step weekly to a year, and CVA, DVA, FVA and FBA read the exposure averaged across each step (§10). On monthly steps with the exposure at each step’s end, a one-month digital-asset forward’s CVA read 31% above daily steps; it is now within 4%.

1.17 (12 November 2026). KVA and MVA charge the whole life of a trade (§10): the remaining life is read at the middle of each grid step, not at its end. Short currency and digital-asset trades were undercharged (a one-month trade by half).

1.16 (12 November 2026). A digital-asset forward that fixes before it is paid is priced to its fixing date and discounted from its payment date (§13, fixings and settlement); the limit of seven days between the two dates is gone.

1.15 (12 November 2026). Volatility regimes of a digital asset (§9). A digital asset’s volatility on any day is the ticket’s times a fast state (calm or stressed, a stress of two or three days) times a slow state (low or high, held about two months), each scaled so that the variance expected over any period is the ticket’s. Today’s value of a forward or an option does not change and an uncollateralised ticket moves little (CVA and FVA 1 to 3% lower on short tickets); over a margin period the tails are fatter, as five years of daily closes show them, and on a margined ticket the margin at the first date rises 7 to 13%. Currency pairs keep one volatility. Three equations added, so the displays after them are numbered three higher.

1.14 (11 November 2026). The value a margin period earlier on currency and digital-asset tickets (§9). The forward’s level is bridged between grid dates in logs, where it is a Brownian motion, and every leg is valued on it; until this version the value itself was bridged as if Gaussian, which read the margin called 9 to 18% low at volatilities of 55 to 110%. Margined figures on those tickets move: on a six-month BTCUSD forward at 55% under a bilateral CSA, KVA −150.7→−134.8, MVA −615.5→−622.1, CVA −2.8→−3.6; at a currency’s volatility by about 1%. The rates ticket and the netting-set engine are unchanged.

1.13 (11 November 2026). Forward curves to ten years (§12). Beyond the last quoted tenor a forward is parity plus the basis that tenor shows, held flat as a rate; until this version the last points were held flat. Every forward says whether it is quoted, interpolated or implied, and how. A tenor can be switched off. One equation added, so the displays after it are numbered one higher.

1.12 (10 November 2026). Typesetting, and one correction. No formula changed. The names of quantities are set upright, displays that ran past the margin are set on several lines, the longest paragraphs are divided, code names are printed as they are written, and this history follows the contents. Corrected: the known limitations of §16 still described the initial-margin method that version 1.10 removed.

1.10 and 1.11 (10 November 2026). Initial margin as the desk’s own amount or the engine’s estimate, with no licensed margin methodology computed or claimed, and the capital add-on of a currency or digital-asset ticket by its own SA-CCR class (§9); wrong-way risk and a package of legs as one netting set (§10); a package of trades confirmed as one record (§17).

1.9 (9 November 2026, evening). The ticket’s scenario tab for a currency forward (§13, digital assets): it starts from the engine’s own forward and carries a rate shock from the spot date, which the pricer’s answer now names; where it is the engine priced again and where it is not is stated.

1.8 (9 November 2026, later). Value and expiry dates by market convention, the calendars against QuantLib, CRYBASIS01 in place of FUND01 on the ticket (§12, §13, §14); the exotic pricer at its limits and the first-passage value in logarithms (§13); a strike booked as displayed.
1.7 (9 November 2026). Fixings for digital assets and settlement on the source the record names (§13).

1.6 (9 November 2026). The first run of the model validator on the venue surface: measured sizes for what the three-point smile, the tenor grid and the two day counts leave out, a corrected statement of the ATM convention at high vols, and the limits of FUND01 and of the built volatility history (§13, §14); no formula changed.

1.5 (9 November 2026). Digital-asset volatility surfaces and forwards are read from a venue’s public option marks in place of the parametric surface and the flat funding rate; the reading, its safeguards and the effect on the volatility history are in §13 and §14.

1.4 (4 November 2026). Collateral as a first-class object: instruments with a yield source, the schedule per counterparty, the regime derived from it, and the carry of the variation margin (ColVA) in the waterfall (§16). Version 1.3 (3 November 2026) added collateral regimes, SA-CCR by asset class, the capital leg and independent price verification.

1.2 (2 November 2026). FX options in every style and the digital-asset options on the same engine (§13); volatility surfaces as risk factors in VaR and stress, and the market-risk and counterparty-credit chapters (§14, §15), which the previous version left to the repository’s notes; the open-box replications and the XVA workbook that carries the engine’s own Monte Carlo draws (§9). Version 1.1 (1 November 2026) added the QuantLib reference suite (§18).

blocks.html: Rijeka is a front-to-back desk for over-the-counter derivatives: booking, pricing, cashflows, risk, XVA under a credit support annex with initial margin, and bilateral confirmation anchored to Ethereum. Phase 1 covers interest-rate products on overnight-index curves (USD SOFR, EUR €STR, GBP SONIA and others) and non-deliverable digital-asset forwards and options.
Three principles govern the implementation.

items.html: No black boxes. Each number is traceable to a formula in this document and a function in the repository; the Excel replications reproduce it outside the system.

One risk taxonomy. Rate sensitivities are per basis point and spot sensitivities per 1%. Sensitivities are IR01 (all curves bumped), IR01_DISC (discount curves only), THETA, GAMMA, VEGA; the terms PV01 and DV01 are not used.
Market data is dated and sourced. Every snapshot carries a valuation date and a source. Pricing off a stale snapshot is permitted but is always flagged with the snapshot date; it is never silent.

blocks.html: Business-day adjustment is Modified Following on the currency’s calendar unless the trade says otherwise. Spot lag is two business days for USD, EUR, JPY and CHF, one for CAD, zero for GBP, AUD and NZD (pricing/bootstrap.py, CCY_SPOT_LAG).
Instruments

A curve is built from an overnight deposit and a strip of OIS par swap rates (tenors in weeks, months and years). Futures, FRAs and IRS quote types are accepted by the engine but Phase 1 curves use deposit and OIS swaps only.
Algorithm

items.html: The overnight deposit gives P(t0​+1d)=1/(1+rON​τACT/360​).

The spot discount factor P(ts​) is obtained by extrapolating the overnight zero rate to the spot date and is frozen as an explicit pillar. This is the step that makes the bootstrap and the pricer agree to the last cent: both read the same P(ts​).

Annual OIS swaps are bootstrapped on a dense integer-year grid (1Y to the longest quote, each year counted from the spot date, so a 29 February spot rolls to 28 February), with missing years filled by linear interpolation of par rates, so that every annual period end is a pillar. This gap fill is a convention: QuantLib’s bootstrap of the same quotes interpolates log-linearly in discount factors between quoted maturities, and the two curves agree at the quotes but part by up to 1.3bp in zero rate (and 4bp in a single three-month forward) between them (§18).
Week- and month-tenor swaps are then bootstrapped in maturity order against the pillars already present.

blocks.html: For an OIS swap of par rate R with annual periods (Ti−1​,Ti​], i=1…n, accrual factors τi​ (ACT/360 for USD), the terminal discount factor solves the par condition with the floating leg replaced by its telescoping value P(ts​)−P(Tn​):
P(Tn​)=1+Rτn​P(ts​)−R∑i=1n−1​τi​P(Ti​)​.(1)
Because every period end is a pillar, a swap struck at its own par rate reprices to exactly zero.
Interpolation and extrapolation
Between pillar dates d0​<d<d1​ the discount factor is log-linear in the calendar-day fraction w=(d−d0​)/(d1​−d0​):
P(d)=exp[(1−w)lnP(d0​)+wlnP(d1​)],(2)

equivalent to a piecewise-constant forward rate. Beyond the last pillar the continuously-compounded zero rate is held flat. Before the first pillar P=1. The Excel replications implement exactly this rule with MATCH/INDEX, so a reader can check any discount factor the engine produces.
Risk bumps
A parallel shift of b basis points is applied to zero rates: Pb​(T)=P(T)e−b⋅10−4T with T in ACT/365F years (Curve.shifted).

blocks.html: Coupon periods are rolled from an anchor at the payment frequency (monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, annual, or zero-coupon), every date counted from the anchor (anchor±k periods) so that a month-end does not drift: rolled back quarterly from 31 August the dates are 31 May, 28 February, 30 November, 31 August. No end-of-month rule is applied. The stub type chooses the anchor: SHORT_FRONT (the default) and LONG_FRONT roll backward from maturity, SHORT_BACK and LONG_BACK forward from the effective date, the long variants merging the odd period into its neighbour; explicit first-period-start and last-period-end dates override this.

Period end dates are unadjusted; payment dates apply the business-day convention and the payment lag in business days of the leg’s calendar (its payment_calendar, else its currency’s: New York, TARGET, London, Tokyo, Zurich, Sydney, Toronto, or a join of them). Floating fixings are two business days before the period start on the same calendar. A period whose accrual ends on a weekend at month-end is therefore paid on the preceding business day, before its accrual ends; QuantLib, which adjusts accrual dates as ISDA does, would not build such a coupon, and the reference checks reproduce it coupon by coupon.

(Before November 2026 the dates drifted after a short month, the stub type was ignored, and the lag and fixing dates counted weekdays only; NPV moved by less than 0.02bp of notional, individual coupon dates by up to three days.)
A fixed coupon over (ds​,de​] is Nrτ(ds​,de​). A floating coupon on a compounded overnight index is projected from the forecast curve as
rfloat​=τ(ds​,de​)1​(Pf​(de​)Pf​(ds​)​−1)+s,(3)

which equals the daily-compounded in-arrears rate implied by the curve; s is the spread. For a period already in progress, a realised fixing R (when supplied) covers the elapsed part τe​ and the curve’s forward F the remainder τr​, compounded: r=[(1+Rτe​)(1+Fτr​)−1]/τ. The realised part is rebuilt from the desk’s own market data (pricing/fixings.py): the overnight rate is the ON quote of every daily snapshot of the leg’s curve, carried over days without a snapshot and compounded on the index’s basis (ACT/360 for SOFR, € STR and SARON, ACT/365F for SONIA and TONA); the price response names the snapshots it used. Without a snapshot on or before the period start the elapsed days are assumed to have accrued at the remaining stub’s forward, and the response says so (the error is the realised-minus-forward gap times the elapsed fraction: 11bp of notional in the reference test, where they differ by 40bp). Notional, fixed-rate and spread schedules (step-ups, amortisation) are resolved per period from their effective dates.

Each coupon is discounted at its business-day-adjusted payment date, the date the cash moves. (Engine versions before October 2026 discounted at the unadjusted period end; where a date rolled over a weekend the two differ by a day or two of discounting. Corrected in v0.5, with the Excel replications as the independent check.)

blocks.html: The value of a leg is the signed sum of discounted coupons, PV=±∑k​Ck​P(Tk​), with pay legs negative. A swap’s NPV is the sum of its legs; a basis swap is two floating legs on different forecast curves; an OIS swap is the single-curve case where forecast and discount curves coincide. The par rate is R∗=PVfloat​/(N∑i​τi​P(Ti​)).
Sensitivities are computed by bump-and-reprice:

items.html: IR01: all curves shifted +1bp;

IR01_DISC: discount curves shifted +1bp with forecasting held fixed (in single-curve mode this requires a separate bumped copy for discounting, so that IR01_DISC < IR01; the difference is the forecasting sensitivity);
THETA: NPV(t0​+1d)−NPV(t0​) with curves held;
GAMMA: second difference of ±1bp shifts.

blocks.html: A swaption under a scenario of its curve or its volatility (the ticket’s scenario tab) is described with the caps’, in §6 (Scenario).

The figures on a ticket carry its side: every figure of money or of risk on a written swaption is the holder’s with the sign turned: the value, vega, the forward delta and the curve’s, gamma, theta, volga, vanna, the hedge notional and the model’s cross-check value; a ratio or a volatility is not (since version 1.42; until then the ticket and its scenario showed the holder’s on either side, so a written option read as an asset and its premium received was added to it; the booked trade’s value and its exposure run already carried the side). The option is priced on the swap it delivers between that swap’s two dates, the fixed leg taken as paid annually on ACT/360 against the index flat, whatever conventions are written on the legs: the ticket shows those terms as they are priced and booked and does not open them, and offers no cap or floor on the delivered swap’s leg, which no swaption pricer reads.
Annuity, forward and the Bachelier price

For an option expiring at Te​ into a swap paying annually at T1​<⋯<Tn​ (dates rolled backward from the swap’s maturity, with the trade’s spot lag and business-day adjustment when the trade dates are supplied),
A=i=1∑n​τi​P(Ti​),F=AP(T0​)−P(Tn​)​.(4)
Rates on overnight curves can be negative and are quoted in normal volatility, so the option is priced in the Bachelier model. With v=σN​Te​​ and d=(F−K)/v,
Vpayer​=NAv[dΦ(d)+φ(d)],Vreceiver​=NAv[−dΦ(−d)+φ(d)].(5)

Greeks are produced by bump-and-reprice: vega per 1bp of σN​, IR01, theta per calendar day, volga, vanna, dollar gamma, and a delta-hedge notional. A Hull–White cross-check price is reported alongside when the model is calibrated (§7).
The expiry on a ticket

The expiry is a tenor or a date. A tenor (1M, 3M, 6M, 9M, 1Y, 2Y, 3Y, 4Y, 5Y, 7Y, 10Y) is that many calendar months from the valuation date, on the same day of the month; a date on a Saturday or a Sunday is moved to the Monday after or, where that is in the next month, to the Friday before. The ticket holds no holiday calendar: an expiry that would fall on a holiday is typed as the date wanted. A typed date is taken as typed; one that is not after the valuation date is refused, in words, and nothing is priced or booked on it.

The option’s time is Te​=d/365 with d the calendar days from the valuation date to the expiry, on a ticket as in the revaluation of the booked option for P&L, VaR and the ladder (§14), so a ticket and its booking are one number and a booked option opened later shows the time it has left. Until version 1.39 a ticket priced a tenor at its nominal fraction of a year. At the money the price is proportional to Te​​, so the change is (d/365)/Tnominal​​−1: nothing for a one-year option over 365 days (+0.14% over the 366 of a year with a 29 February in it), +0.41% for three months of 92 days, +0.21% for two years of 733 days (a leap day and a weekend’s roll), +0.04% for ten years of 3,653 days. That is the time alone, at the money: the forward and the annuity move with the delivered swap’s dates by a day or two as well, and away from the money the smile is read at the new time. The exposure paths measure the same option’s time in years of 365.25 days (§15): 0.07% less time, a stated difference between the two engines.

The swap delivered starts as many calendar days after the spot-starting swap of the same tenor as the expiry is after the valuation date, which keeps the trade’s spot lag after the expiry, and ends its tenor later by the calendar. Until version 1.39 both dates were moved by one count of days, which ended a five-year swap one day short whenever a 29 February fell inside it. Neither date is adjusted for a weekend or a holiday in the ticket’s price (a start on a Saturday is priced from the Saturday; the booked legs carry a business-day convention for their own schedules): a stated limit, not sized. A booked trade keeps its dates: opened again, its ticket reads the expiry from the booked terms and the delivered swap from the booked legs, whichever rule made them; past its expiry it is that swap, and no option is priced.
The ticket’s date rule has no reference comparison and no workbook: it is covered by unit tests asserted by hand (product-defaults.test.js), and the model inventory says so.

A Bermudan (§7) takes a tenor only and whole years for its time, on a new ticket and on a booked one: its tree steps in twelfths of a year, while its expiry date and the swap’s dates are the calendar’s, a day or three apart from the tree’s at the last exercise.
Volatility tiers

A swaption is priced at the volatility in its request or, when the request carries none, at the one the desk’s market gives: the point of the currency’s at-the-money grid nearest the option, nearest in ∣ln(Te​/Te′​)∣+∣ln(τ/τ′)∣ over the grid’s expiries Te′​ and swap tenors τ′ (an expiry under one month counts as one month and a tenor under three months as three). There is no interpolation between points, and beyond the grid’s edges the edge stands: a three-month expiry reads the one-year row. The point is read on the latest market date at or before the valuation date, so the same option can read another point, or another level, on another day. A ticket sends no volatility unless one is typed; it shows the number in its volatility field before it is priced, with the point and the surface’s date under it.

The same lookup revalues the booked option for P&L, VaR and the ladder (§14) and gives the market volatility reported beside an exposure run (§15). So, at the money, on the day, an untouched ticket and its booking are valued at one volatility; over the ticket’s lists of expiries and tenors the two ask for the same point on every weekday of two years (the validator’s sweep; a typed expiry date and the exposure engine’s question were not swept). Away from the money they differ where a smile is stored: the ticket’s price is then struck at the smile’s volatility, also over a typed one, while the booked option is revalued at the at-the-money point. Where no smile is stored a strike away from the money is priced flat at the at-the-money volatility. Both are stated limits.

The volatility is tagged. MANUAL: the request’s own. QUOTED: read from the grid, the option on a grid point, which is within two per cent of it in the distance above (a year by the calendar is 365 to 368 days, and is the one-year point on every trade date). NEAREST: read from the grid’s nearest point, the option off it. DEFAULT: the currency has no surface, and the desk default of 85bp stands in. SABR, or the name the stored smile’s parameters carry: a strike away from the money, priced at the smile’s volatility, which the answer reports beside the at-the-money one. The tier travels with the price, with the point and the surface’s date, so that a valuation can be challenged; under a scenario’s volatility shift they describe the point before the shift. Only the dollar has a surface in the hosted demo, and it is synthetic (§14); a swaption in another currency is priced at the default unless a volatility is typed, and the ticket says so. The lookup is the desk’s own rule: it has no reference comparison and no workbook, only unit tests asserted by hand and the validator’s independent sweep. Until version 1.40 a ticket with no volatility typed was priced at 86.5bp whatever the expiry, the tenor or the day.
β=0 normal SABR
The smile at each expiry–tenor point is the normal SABR of Hagan et al. (2002) with backbone β=0:
σN​(K)C​=αC(F,K){1+[242−3ρ2​ν2+4ρνα​]T},=χ(z)z​,z=αν​(F−K),χ(z)=ln1−ρ1−2ρz+z2​+z−ρ​,​(6)

with C=1 at the money. Parameters (α,ρ,ν) are fitted to quoted volatilities at strike offsets {−200,−100,−50,−25,0,+25,+50,+100,+200}bp by weighted least squares, with α constrained so the at-the-money volatility is matched exactly. The fit RMSE is stored with the parameters.

blocks.html: A cap on a compounded overnight index is a strip of caplets on the periods of the floating leg it is booked as (Booking, below): from the leg’s effective date to its maturity (on a ticket the currency’s spot date and the tenor in calendar months, or the dates typed), at its payment frequency, with its day count on the accruals between unadjusted dates, each caplet paid on the adjusted end of its period plus the index’s payment lag. The price on a ticket and the value of the booked trade are this one calculation on the same leg (api/routes/pricer.py, \_cap\_like; pricing/ir\_swap.py), and a test holds the ticket’s price to the stored trade’s value to the cent. Until version 1.42 the ticket priced a schedule of its own: quarterly from two calendar days after the valuation date, which could be a Saturday, on ACT/360 whatever the ticket’s day count, discounted at each period’s end, and the dates typed on the ticket were not read. At one volatility (85bp, on the reference suite’s curve, three five-year options measured before the change) the two were 0.1 to 0.2% of the premium apart on the ticket’s own terms and 4 to 6.5% once the day count was changed to 30/360 or ACT/365F; a start date typed three months on changed the booking and not the price. The rate fixes in arrears over the whole period; the caplet is valued with option time to the middle of its accrual period, T=[(ds​−t0​)+21​(de​−ds​)]/365 (option_time; the market’s convention for a cap on a compounded overnight rate). Time is on ACT/365F because normal vols are quoted per 365-day year; before November 2026 it was measured on ACT/360, which overstated the variance by 365/360. For caplet (ds​,de​] with forward F from (3) and normal volatility σN​,
caplet=NτP(dp​)[(F−K)Φ(d)+σN​T​φ(d)],d=σN​T​F−K​,(7)

with dp​ the date the caplet is paid, and a floorlet is the corresponding put. The at-the-money strike of a cap is the annuity-weighted average of its caplet forwards; a cap or a floor whose strike is left blank on a ticket is struck there, to eight decimals, the price says so and the booking carries that rate (a collar has no strike to take from the market: both are typed). A collar is a long cap and a short floor. The figures carry the side: a written option’s value, vega and rate risk are the holder’s with the sign turned, and a written collar is the floor held and the cap written (until version 1.42 the ticket showed the holder’s figures on either side). A cap’s flat volatility is read from the surface at the strike’s distance from the at-the-money forward, on straight lines through the quoted distances and the at-the-money quote and on the last line beyond them; the distance is signed, and a floor is read at the same point as a cap at its strike. It is a continuous function of the forward. The surface is quoted at a few cap maturities (one, two, three, five, seven and ten years), and an option is read at its remaining life, from the valuation date to the leg’s maturity in years of 365.25 days: within a hundredth of a year of a quoted maturity, there; between two, at the strike’s distance from the money on each and on the straight line in maturity between the two; shorter than the first or longer than the last, at that end’s. Until version 1.42 a remaining life that was not a quoted maturity fell to the desk’s default of 85bp: a five-year cap booked from its spot date is 5.0103 years from the valuation date, outside that hundredth, inside it for the week after, and outside it from then until its life comes within four days of the next quoted maturity; so a booked cap, and a cap or a floor on a swap’s leg, was valued at the default beside a quoted surface on all but a few days of its life (on the stack’s market the five-year 4.5% cap above at 85bp and 105,015, where the surface gives 81.48bp and 97,322). The straight line in maturity between flat volatilities is the engine’s own choice and has no outside reference. Between two maturities and beyond the ends the reading is labelled interpolated (an end held flat has no label of its own), and the default is named only where a maturity it reads has no quote at all; a maturity with no at-the-money quote takes the default at the money and is labelled by its distances. At the edge of the hundredth the two readings meet to within a two-hundredth of the step between the neighbouring maturities, a few thousandths of a basis point, which is not smoothed. These are the engine’s own conventions and have no independent reference (the reference caps and the workbook are given their volatility; since version 1.45 a floor and a collar have workbooks of their own, floor and collar, each the ticket as it opens on the same leg, a floorlet the put of the caplet’s formula and the collar the cap bought fifty basis points above the at-the-money forward less the floor sold fifty below, every period evaluated outside Excel against the engine’s figure for it to a tenth of a cent, and each with a cell for the side that wrote the option; the workbook cap is the ticket’s own trade as it opens, on the leg’s periods with each caplet paid two business days after its period, its cells evaluated outside Excel against the engine and its engine figure held to the ticket’s route): beyond the last quoted distance the last line carries on, held between 1bp and 500bp; a distance quoted twice counts once, at the mean; one strike has one volatility whichever option is struck there, so that a cap less a floor at one strike is the swap at that strike whatever the volatility; and a surface quoted on one side of the money only is mirrored for a strike on the other side, for a cap as for a floor, where a straight line carried through the money would run on (one quote on a side is enough for that side to be read as quoted, on the line from the money to that quote). The at-the-money forward is that of the option’s own schedule, so one strike on two schedules (a cap on its own and a capped leg whose first periods have run off) can be read a fraction of a basis point apart. Until version 1.24 a floor was read at the size of its distance, so a floor struck below the money took the volatility quoted the same distance above it and a cap and a floor at one strike could be priced at two volatilities. Until version 1.22 the distance was rounded to a whole basis point, a strike within five basis points of the money took the at-the-money volatility and one within a basis point of a quote took that quote; each was a step in the price as the curve moved, and a cap’s rate risk depended on the size of the move it was measured with. QuantLib’s compounded-overnight caplet pricer, which models the backward-looking accrual itself, values the reference caps 0.6–2.0% of premium lower and the reference floor 2.5% higher (§18); that is the size of the mid-period convention. Those reference caps are on a quarterly schedule of the suite’s own (price\_cap, which no route calls since version 1.42) and measure the convention, which is the same formula caplet by caplet; the leg’s strip a ticket and a booking are valued by is compared with QuantLib’s Bachelier formula on the leg’s own dates (booked\_cap\_rows). An index other than the currency’s overnight rate (a term rate, the effective federal funds rate) is forecast off the overnight curve: a ticket prices on one curve a currency, the ticket says so beside the index, and a basis between two indices of one currency is not valued.

Booking. A cap, floor or collar is booked as one floating leg with zero participation in the rate (leverage 0) and the strikes on its embedded_options (a collar: a bought cap and a sold floor, or the reverse), so the swap pricer, the exposure engine and the P&L value exactly the caplet strip; the side, strikes, vol and premium are also in the trade’s terms. A premium is in the terms only where the desk entered one: the model’s value is a mid and is not booked in a premium’s place (until version 1.44 a cap, a floor or a collar with no premium entered was booked with its value as its premium; a swaption with none). A floating leg’s leverage multiplies its projected rate everywhere (booked and ignored before November 2026). Until then these products were booked as a generic two-leg swap with no strike stored.

Scenario. The scenario tab of a rates ticket (a swap, a cap, a floor, a collar, a swaption) is the pricing engine on a moved market; with no shock its request is the request the ticket was priced with and its value the ticket’s. A shock of a curve is a shift of the quotes the curve is built from, in basis points: one for every quote and one of its own for a tenor. The tab shows a curve at its main tenors; a quote between two of them takes the shock on the straight line in time between theirs and the end tenor’s beyond them (a choice of the tab’s, not a market convention), and a quote whose tenor is not a plain tenor takes the flat shock only. The curve is bootstrapped again from the moved quotes and the trade repriced on it in full. The engine takes a shift of at most 1,000bp on a quote and the tab one of at most 300bp. A shock of the volatility is a shift, in basis points of normal volatility, of the volatility the trade is priced at: one for the whole surface and one of its own at a maturity of the cap surface or an expiry of the swaption surface (read at the swap tenor stored nearest the trade’s). The trade takes the shift at its own maturity or expiry, on the straight line in time between the two points around it and the end point’s beyond them; the smile moves in level, not in shape, and a shifted volatility is held at no less than 0.01bp. While the curve moves the trade stays where the saved curve put it: a cap or a floor is read on the surface at its strike’s distance from the saved curve’s at-the-money forward, a swaption struck at the money keeps the strike the saved curve gave, and one away from the money keeps the volatility the surface gave it there (the moved curve does not read the surface again). The change in value under a curve shock is therefore the price on the curve rebuilt from the shifted quotes, at a fixed volatility; under a volatility shock it is the price at the shifted volatility; and what the two together add beyond their sum is shown as a cross term. Beside them the tab shows the ticket’s own IR01 and vega times the shock, which are first-order figures and differ from the repricing by more than curvature: the ticket’s IR01 moves the forwards with the discount factors held (a cap’s, a swaption’s analytic delta) where the scenario moves both, and a quote moved one basis point is not a zero rate moved one basis point. On a flat 3.5% curve a five-year 4% cap at 85bp moves by 3.6% less than its IR01 for one basis point, by 0.5% more than ten of them for ten, and by a fifth more than fifty of them for fifty. A Bermudan swaption is priced on the tree at the model’s own volatility (§7), the σ of the stored calibration, one number with no surface behind it: its volatility shock is a shift of that σ in basis points, held at no less than 0.01bp, and the tree is built again; the vega the ticket reports is the central difference of one basis point either side of the same σ, so a shift of one basis point is the vega to first order, the difference being the tree’s curvature in σ; at the floor no vega is reported, the bump below it being a negative σ. This is not a shift of the swaption surface: that would be the model calibrated again to the moved surface, which the tab does not do, and a basis point of the short rate’s volatility is not a basis point of a swaption’s normal volatility. The tab names the factor Hull–White σ and offers it flat only. A collar’s legs are priced on the ticket’s own periods, as a cap’s and a floor’s are, in a scenario as without one (until 16 November 2026 its route priced them quarterly whatever the ticket said). Since version 1.42 a scenario of a cap, a floor or a collar runs through the leg’s strip (the shift of the volatility and the forward the strike’s place on the smile is held at are handed to it), which has unit tests of its own and no reference row. The three routes take 1, 2, 4 or 12 periods a year, the frequencies a leg is scheduled at, and refuse any other count (three and six went with version 1.42, when the routes took the leg’s schedule). A collar has no outside comparison or workbook of its own: it is the cap less the floor, and a test holds it to them at each frequency. The shifts have no outside reference of their own: the moved market is priced by the functions whose prices are compared with QuantLib (§18). Tests hold that no shift is no change, to the cent; that the saved curve shifted by the engine is the curve of its own quotes shifted and sent; that a volatility shift is the price at the shifted volatility; and, on the test market, that one basis point of curve moves a swap by its IR01 to 2%, a cap, floor or collar by its IR01 to 10% and a swaption by its curve delta to 10% (the tolerance is the discounting and quote-against-zero difference above, so it would not catch an error smaller than that), and one basis point of volatility by the vega to 5%; and that a Bermudan’s price rises with its σ, one basis point either side being the route’s own vega to rounding and one basis point up the vega to 5%, where the test market holds a calibration (the test is skipped where it does not). That test holds the shift to the σ the vega is of; the tree itself is held by its comparison with the Jamshidian closed form (§7).

Caplet volatilities are stripped from flat cap volatilities one strike column at a time: the 1Y bucket is solved so that four Bachelier caplets reproduce the 1Y cap price; each later bucket (2Y, 3Y, 3–5Y, 5–7Y, 7–10Y) is solved after subtracting the value of the buckets already priced, piecewise flat within a bucket. A β=0 SABR smile is then fitted per expiry bucket across strikes.

The label: INTERP between maturities and beyond the ends (an end held flat has no label of its own), FALLBACK only where a maturity read has no rows; a maturity with no at-the-money row takes the 85bp default at the money and is still labelled by its distances; at the edge of the 0.01 the two readings differ by a two-hundredth of the step between the neighbouring maturities (thousandths of a bp, not smoothed). The 0.1 to 0.2 % and 4 to 6.5 % of the methodology were measured before the change on the reference suite's curve at 85bp (price_cap against price_swap on the booked leg, three options, three day counts) and are not held by a test, the old schedule being gone from the routes. A booked cap's value steps on the day of the deploy, and with no cap-vol step in the P&L explain that step is in the residual. The model validator re-derived the workbook's trade with code of the validator's own (QuantLib's calendar for the dates, the curve's discount factors, Bachelier by hand): 239,308.8906 against the engine's 239,308.8906. A written collar's signs are held by a unit test on the leg (TestAWrittenCollar) and by the route's test against the stored trade, which is a consistency test; a scenario's vol shift and held forward through the strip have unit tests (TestAStripUnderAScenario) and no reference row. A caller's leg is checked before the schedule (frequency, day count, roll, lag, at most 60 years). The pinned sample book did not move (its cap is 5.0055 years from its valuation date, inside the old tolerance). A blank strike is at the money (the leg's own forward to eight decimals), the side signs every figure, text that is not a rate or a vol is refused (it priced as 0 % or as nothing typed); 3 and 6 periods a year are refused (a leg is not scheduled at them). blocks.html: Module: pricing/bermudan_swaption.py.

The short rate follows drt​=[θ(t)−art​]dt+σdWt​. Zero-coupon bonds are affine, P(t,T)=A(t,T)e−B(t,T)rt​ with B(t,T)=(1−e−a(T−t))/a (Brigo–Mercurio 2006, eq. 3.39). The tree is the Hull–White (1994) trinomial tree: a symmetric tree in xt​=rt​−α(t) with the standard branching rules, and a deterministic shift α(t) fitted at every grid time by Arrow–Debreu forward induction so that the tree reprices the market discount curve exactly. Backward induction values the underlying swap at each node by the single-curve telescoping identity PVfloat​(t)=∑k​Nk​[P(t,Tk−1​)−P(t,Tk​)], and applies the early-exercise test at each exercise date.

Validation gate. Before any Bermudan value is trusted, the same tree must price European swaptions within 0.5% (at the money) and 1% (±100bp) of the closed-form Bachelier price on a grid of expiries and tenors. Scope. The model is single-curve and single-tenor: multi-curve underlyings, capped or floored underlyings and basis underlyings are refused rather than approximated, and a Bermudan whose underlying tenor is far from the 5Y calibration column carries a warning.
