blocks.html: Simulation

Which volatility. The Hull–White parameters a and σ are calibrated to dollar swaptions, the one swaption surface the system stores. A swap in another currency is discounted and projected on its own curve and simulated on that dollar volatility: there is no market data provider for swaption volatility in other currencies here. Its exposure, and every adjustment read from it, therefore carries dollar rate volatility; the XVA tab of such a swap says so above its figures, and the run’s answer names the surface (vol\_basis).

Short-rate paths are simulated under the calibrated Hull–White model on a monthly grid with the exact fit to the initial curve, and the trade is revalued on every path and date, giving mark-to-market paths V(t) from our side. With r(t)=f(0,t)+ϕ(t)+x(t), x the driftless Ornstein–Uhlenbeck deviation and ϕ(t)=2a2σ2​(1−e−at)2, a bond on a path is
P(t,T)=P(0,t)P(0,T)​exp[−B(t,T)(x(t)+ϕ(t))−4aσ2​B(t,T)2(1−e−2at)],B=a1−e−a(T−t)​.(9)

The counterparty engine (ccr/simulate.py) omitted ϕ(t) until November 2026, which priced bonds high and put path forwards ϕ(t) below the curve (8bp at five years, 27bp at ten, for a=3%, σ=85bp); the risk-neutral martingale check in the reference suite now pins it. Grid times are the grid dates’ distance in 365.25-day years, the clock every trade date uses, so a fixing or expiry on a grid date sits on that grid point. A European swaption on the paths is valued before expiry with Bachelier on each path’s forward swap rate at the normal vol the paths’ own Hull–White model implies for it (the Jamshidian price at t0​ inverted through Bachelier, ccr/options.hw_implied_vol) and exercised at expiry on the same paths, so the value before expiry and the exercise are one model and expected exposure does not step at expiry (with today’s market vol instead it stepped by the ratio of the two vols, 13–25% in the reference test, until November 2026); the market quote is reported beside the vol used. A sold option enters with the opposite sign (the terms’ side).

A cap or a floor on the paths (since version 1.43; ccr/options.value\_caplets). A period (s,e] of a cap pays, on its payment date p, Nmax(G−X,0) with G what one unit placed at s has grown to by e on the path and X=1+τK; a floor pays Nmax(X−G,0). On the paths G is a product of the grid’s own bonds (the account over whole steps, and at each end the bond seen on the grid date before), each the exponential of the factor at its grid date, so lnG is a constant plus ∑k​wk​x(tk​) over grid dates: wk​=B(tk+1​−tk​) for a whole step, less B(s−tk​) at the step the period starts in, and B(e−tk​) at the grid date before its end, with B(u)=(1−e−au)/a. Seen from grid date ti​ the factor at a later date has variance 2aσ2​(1−e−2a(tk​−ti​)) and the dates after it follow it decayed, so
vi2​=Var[lnG∣x(ti​)]=k>i∑​2aσ2​(1−e−2a(tk​−ti​))wk​(wk​+2Sk​),Sk​=l>k∑​wl​e−a(tl​−tk​).(10)

Under the measure of the period’s end the mean of G is what the path’s bonds give: M=P(t,s)/P(t,e) before the period begins and M=G(s,t)/P(t,e) while it runs, G(s,t) being the growth so far. The caplet is then Black’s formula on the growth factor,
Vcaplet​(t)=NP(t,p)[MΦ(d1​)−XΦ(d1​−vi​)],d1​=vi​ln(M/X)+21​vi2​​,(11)

the floorlet the corresponding put, and once the period has ended and waits for its payment date, Nmax(G−X,0)P(t,p) with the growth the path has realised. A payment after the period’s end is discounted to its date as a swap’s floating coupon is; the two days’ convexity is not in it. On the risk-neutral paths, which are a ticket’s run and the pricing run of a netting set, the factor is normal and nothing in this is approximated but the payment lag: the value before a period, during it and at its end are one formula, so the value discounted along the path is a martingale and expected exposure does not step when a period fixes. On the real-world paths of a netting set’s risk measures (§15), whose increments are drawn from history and whose drift is not the curve’s, the growth is not exactly normal and the formula is the value given the path’s state under the pricing model, as a swap’s is there. The payment lag is approximated in two places: the caplet is discounted from its payment date with the bond to that date in place of the measure of that date, and its payment is set in the grid step that holds the payment date with no interest to the step’s end (the convexity of two days is under 0.03%; the second was not measured). A collar is its cap less its floor on every path, and at one strike a cap less a floor is the swap’s floating coupons less the strike’s, path by path (both tested). What a period pays is in the cash paid on the path (caplet\_flows), so a margined run sets it against the margin period’s move as it does a coupon. Until version 1.43 a caplet on a swap’s leg was Bachelier on the path’s forward at the market’s at-the-money cap volatility until the period’s start, and the payoff of that forward after: a rate fixed in advance where the product fixes in arrears, at a volatility that was not the paths’ own, and its payment was in no cash flow; a cap, a floor and a collar were not valued at all.

What the figure is of, and is not. The variance is the model’s, calibrated to swaptions, not the volatility the ticket prices the cap at: the run prints beside the cap the one normal volatility at which the ticket’s formula (§6) would give the model’s value today, and the volatility the ticket prices at (on the stack’s market 71.0bp against 81.5bp for the five-year 4.5% cap, whose paths therefore start about a fifth below its price; at the money 70.8bp against 78.3bp, about a tenth). The exposure is then of the model’s cap, not the market’s: with a market volatility above the model’s it is understated, by something of the order of that ratio for a cap at the money, whose value is close to proportional to the volatility, and by more for one out of the money; the size was not measured along the profile. A swaption’s exposure has the same limit. The paths carry the rate’s variance at their monthly dates only: inside a step the account grows at the rate seen at the step’s start, so the first step of a period carries no variance of its own. A quarterly period therefore has less variance than the continuous model gives it, and much less when it is near: seen from today, 44% less for a period that starts today, 11% three months on, 6.5% six months on, 3.5% a year on, 1.9% two years on and 1.3% three (the model validator’s figures, a=3%, σ=85bp; a ratio, so it does not depend on σ). The near periods of a cap, which carry little of its value, are the ones most understated. The caplet is valued at the paths’ own variance so that it stays a martingale on them, and stands 0.7 to 3.9% below the continuous Hull–White price in the reference comparison (periods one to three years on, §18). A finer grid would close this; it is not done. On a ticket the capital add-on of a cap is on its whole notional, with no adjustment for the option’s delta, as a swaption’s is there. In a netting set’s capital (§16) a cap and a floor each enter as one option on the rate with the supervisory delta of CRE52.40 and their own side (a cap a call, a floor a put; bought, the cap is long the rate and the floor short it), on the forward of the strip’s own periods and exercised at its last period’s start: one row an option, not a row a caplet, which is this engine’s reading and is stated in the report’s notes. A sold cap on a swap’s leg, five years at 4.5% on ten million on a flat 3.75% curve (a=3%, σ=80bp, 20,000 paths, seeds 42, 7 and 11), shows a mean exposure against us over its life of −57,900 to −58,300 where the valuation before version 1.43, at the 85bp it then read, showed −62,500 to −62,900: 7.3 to 7.4% less, and 15% less at the peak.

A rates ticket values the trade itself (since version 1.34). The run is given the trade as it would be booked, or a stored trade’s id, and values its legs on the paths by the valuation of §15: each fixed coupon on its payment date, each floating period on its own dates with the interest accrued so far, a swaption as the option to its expiry and the swap after, on the run’s own curve and the run’s (a,σ), monthly from the valuation date to the month after the last payment. The grid is monthly by the calendar and the waterfall takes one step length, the mean one. The value at the start of the paths is the paths’ own and is reported beside the pricer’s value of the trade; the paths are not moved to meet the pricer (on the pinned five-year swap the two stand 68 apart on a value of −122,568), and the all-in figure is the pricer’s value and the adjustments. A netting set that holds this trade alone, on the same date, paths and spreads, is the same calculation: the two agree within 0.2% on CVA, DVA, FCA and FBA, within 0.5% on KVA, and date by date on expected exposure (tests/integration/test\_xva\_reconcile.py). Until version 1.34 the ticket valued a swap of the ticket’s notional, coupon and original tenor whose two legs settle every month, V=±N(K∑j​ΔP(t,tj​)−(1−P(t,T))), moved to the pricer’s value by a re-strike: near its end a swap that pays yearly still has a year’s net coupon at stake and that swap showed almost none; a stored trade was run at its original tenor, not what is left of it; and a swaption’s expiry, tenor and volatility were sent and not read, so its figures were a swap’s (on a one-year into five-year payer, a DVA more than three times the option’s). That swap is still what the xva\_rates workbook rebuilds cell by cell, and what a request that carries no trade is answered with; the answer then says so. An outside figure for the exposure. On a coupon date a swap is what is left of it, so the discounted expected positive value of a receive-fixed swap at that date is today’s price of a receiver swaption expiring then into the remaining swap, and what is owed is the payer swaption’s. The engine’s E[D(t)max(±V(t),0)] on its own paths stands within 1.3% of QuantLib’s Jamshidian price under the same Hull–White parameters and curve at every yearly date of a six-year swap, both sides, and within two standard errors (ten rows of the reference suite, §18; the model validator’s own run on a flat curve at 100,000 paths: within 0.4%). A swaption’s discounted value on the paths before its expiry stands within 0.7% of the QuantLib price today (the validator, four seeds), the cost of valuing it by Bachelier at the model’s implied volatility. These are the first figures for an exposure from outside this code; since version 1.35 unilateral CVA and DVA have theirs (§10).

Replication of a cap’s run (version 1.43). The workbook xva\_cap is the same book for a bought two-year quarterly cap as the cap ticket books it: a Variance sheet rebuilds (10) for each period from each grid date, and per period and path the sheet rebuilds M and the caplet per unit, the value, the cash paid; the exposure, the margin and the waterfall are the swap book’s own sheets. Its cells against the engine’s figures on the same draws, evaluated outside Excel: every comparison of its Checks sheet (114 to 117: the value today, the variance of a period’s growth, the caplet per unit on a path, figures on single paths, the exposure at every date, every charge) under each margin preset and with typed terms, on five valuation dates, the largest relative difference seen 5×10−11; and its engine figures against the ticket’s route for the same cap, parameters, paths and seed, to the cent under each preset. The book was opened in Excel by the project’s owner on 19 November 2026 and every row of its Checks sheet read PASS; its builder has not opened it in Excel. It is one bought cap.

Replication of a floor’s and a collar’s run (version 1.45). The workbooks xva\_floor and xva\_collar are the cap’s book for a bought two-year quarterly floor and for a collar, each as its ticket books it. A floor’s period is the put on the growth: before it ends XΦ(v−d1​)−MΦ(−d1​) per unit, after it max(X−G,0). The collar holds the cap, struck fifty basis points above the floor’s book’s strike, and has written the floor, struck fifty below: each strip is valued at its own strike, the floor’s periods count against the holder of the cap, and the value of the set takes both signs, so DVA and FBA are charged where a bought option has none. A written option on the paths is therefore in a book. Each book’s cells against the engine’s figures on the same draws, evaluated outside Excel: every comparison of its Checks sheet (114 for the floor, 115 for the collar) under each margin preset and 258 with typed terms, on five valuation dates, the largest relative difference seen 7×10−11; and the engine’s figures against the ticket’s route for the same trade, parameters, paths and seed, to the cent under each preset. Neither book has been opened in Excel itself yet.

Replication of a swaption’s run (version 1.45). The workbook xva\_swaption is the run of a swaption ticket’s XVA tab for a bought payer swaption, one year into a two-year swap, as the swaption ticket books it: the option’s terms beside the swap delivered, which starts as many days after a spot-starting swap as the expiry is after the valuation date. Until the expiry the trade is the option: on each path at each date the annuity A=∑τk​P(t,Tk​) over the fixed leg and the forward swap rate F=(P(t,T0​)−P(t,Tn​))/A from the path’s own bonds, and NAσn​Te​−t​[dΦ(d)+φ(d)] with d=(F−K)/(σn​Te​−t​). At the first grid date on or after the expiry the swap delivered is valued on its own schedule; on the paths where it is worth having there the trade is that swap from then on, with its coupons as payments, and on the others it is nothing. An Option sheet rebuilds σn​: the model’s exact price of the swaption (Jamshidian: the level x∗ of the factor at which the fixed leg’s payments are worth one unit, and the option as the sum of options on the bonds those payments are, each struck at that bond’s price at x∗), and the one normal volatility at which Bachelier’s formula on today’s forward swap rate gives that price per unit of annuity. The level and the volatility are the engine’s roots and stand in the sheet as values; the sheet shows that each is a root. The value the run starts from is therefore the model’s own price of the option, not the price the ticket shows at the market’s quote. Its cells against the engine’s figures on the same draws, evaluated outside Excel: every comparison of its Checks sheet (163 to 166: the bonds’ prices at x∗, the model’s price, the volatility’s own check, the annuity and the forward swap rate on a path, the swap delivered at the expiry on a path that exercises and on one that does not, the exposure at every date, every charge) under each margin preset and 366 to 375 with typed terms, on five valuation dates, every relative difference below 3×10−11; and the engine’s figures against the ticket’s route for the same swaption, parameters, paths and seed, to the cent under each preset. The value today was also derived by the model validator with code of his own that does not use the decomposition (the payoff integrated over the factor at the expiry): 79,533.155425 against the engine’s 79,533.155424 on the test market. The book has not been opened in Excel itself yet. Not in it: a written swaption and a receiver (the formulas for both are written and have not been evaluated against the engine: the book is one bought payer), and a Bermudan, whose exposure is run as its European’s.

A difference inside the run, found by this replication. The price the run starts from treats the swap as starting on the expiry date: its floating leg is 1−P(Te​,Tn​). The swap the paths exercise into starts on its own start date, two business days later: P(Te​,T0​)−P(Te​,Tn​). In the same model the option on the swap as delivered is worth about 1.5% less than the price the run starts from (78,306 against 79,533 on the test market, for this trade), so the value before the expiry and the mean of what the paths deliver at it differ by that. The workbook reproduces the engine as it is. The engine is to be changed to price the option on the swap from its own start; until then a swaption’s exposure before its expiry is high by about that share.

Replication (since version 1.41). The workbook xva\_rates rebuilds this run for a two-year swap from spot, both legs yearly, taken through the ticket’s own booking path: the factor on the grid’s dates, the bond over each step and to each of the trade’s dates, the account, each floating period’s growth, the value by the cases above, the cash paid, each path’s discounting over the curve’s, the value a margin period back, and the waterfall of §10 on the path-discounted exposure. Two comparisons stand behind it. Its cells against the engine’s figures on the same draws, evaluated outside Excel by a formula library (scripts/check\_workbook.py): every comparison of its Checks sheet (over a hundred: the value today, figures on single paths, the exposure at every date, every charge) under each margin preset, on five valuation dates and a sloped curve, and at the book’s own 200 paths, the largest relative difference seen 2×10−10; and, because the presets have no threshold, minimum transfer amount, margin yield or carry and one capital model, the same with those terms typed into the sheet, a wrong-way multiplier and each capital model in turn, against the engine under the same terms. And the engine’s figures it carries against the ticket’s route for the same trade, parameters, paths and seed: every charge and the exposure at every date to the cent, on the book’s own inputs (the snapshot’s curve and date, the parameters the book fitted or read). The model validator recomputed the value on every path, the weights and the four exposure charges with code of the validator’s own, to twelve digits. The book was opened in Excel by the project’s owner on 18 November 2026 and every row of its Checks sheet read PASS; its builder has not opened it in Excel. In the project’s automated checks the cells are not evaluated (the library is not a requirement of the project), only the comparison with the route. It is one trade on its default credit and funding inputs: a swaption on the paths, a trade already running, fees and wrong-way risk are not in the book.

Not done, and to be read with every figure of a rates ticket: the capital add-on of a swaption, and of a cap, a floor or a collar, is read on its whole notional, with no adjustment for the option’s delta, and a forward-starting trade’s on its life to maturity; a Bermudan swaption is run as its European; an option on the paths is valued at the volatility the paths’ own model implies, not the ticket’s (the market’s quote is reported beside it), so its value at the start of the paths differs from the pricer’s by that much; a trade already running starts on the paths with its past floating interest at today’s rate, not its fixings, so its start differs from the pricer’s by about the notional times the gap between the two rates times the time elapsed; a swap in another currency carries dollar volatility (above); a grid date that falls a day or two before a coupon’s payment date (a weekend) shows the exposure with that coupon still to come, about a quarter higher than its neighbours on a five-year swap, which matters for a peak and for cents of CVA; the step is the mean month, so dates are up to two and a half days off (−0.04% on the CVA of a five-year swap, the validator’s figure) and the margin period’s share of a short month is misread; the trade’s own paths have no workbook yet.
Variation margin and the margin period of risk
Variation margin held at t was called against the exposure one margin period of risk δ earlier:
C(t)=max(V(t−δ)−THcp​,0)−max(−V(t−δ)−THown​,0),(12)
zeroed when ∣C∣ is below the minimum transfer amount. The margin period δ is shorter than a grid step, so V(t−δ) is sampled from the Brownian bridge between grid points,
V(t−δ)​V(t−Δt),V(t)∼N(V(t−Δt)+wΔV,w(1−w)s2),w=ΔtΔt−δ​,(13)
with s2 the cross-path variance of ΔV. This preserves the variance of the move over the margin period; linear interpolation would understate it by a factor δ/Δt.

The bridge above is between values and is Gaussian whatever the value is. On a currency or digital-asset ticket (§12) the value is a function of one lognormal level, every forward of the pair being Fi​(0)Mt​, and the bridge is taken where it is exact (since v1.14). Inside a grid step lnM is a Brownian motion with that step’s volatility σj​, so
lnM(t−δ)​lnM(t−Δt),lnM(t)∼N(lnM(t−Δt)+wΔlnM,σj2​w(1−w)Δt),(14)

and each leg is valued on that level with the time it then has left: a forward as ±N(F0​M(t−δ)−K)DFq​(t−δ,T), an option by its style’s closed form, a barrier or a touch carrying what the grid dates before it have seen. A leg that has settled stands at the amount it paid; before today the value is today’s. A margin period of a whole number of steps reads the grid itself. Two approximations are the paths’ own. In the step that ends on the expiry’s grid date the time left runs to that date, where the paths fix the payoff, not to the expiry. And a barrier or a touch carries the knock state of the grid dates before t−δ and is then valued by a closed form that monitors continuously: a path beyond the barrier at t−δ that has not knocked on the grid is valued as knocked, though about a third of such paths are back inside at the next grid date, which overstates the move near the barrier (by about 13% of the margin called at one date of a six-month up-barrier at 115% of spot and 80% volatility) until the paths monitor between grid dates. The rates ticket and the netting-set engine (§15) keep the bridge between values. Functions exact_lag, lagged_values.

Replication of a forward’s run (version 1.46). The workbooks xva\_fx and xva\_crypto are the run of a forward ticket’s XVA tab: buy EUR 10m, or 10 BTC cash-settled in USD, eighteen months forward at the fair forward. The forward, its discount factor and its spot sensitivity are the ones the ticket’s route reads from the account’s market (the pair’s stored spot, curves and points, the spot date), and at eighteen months the ticket’s own grid is the monthly one the book is written on (nineteen steps where the settlement, eighteen months from the spot date, is a little over a year and a half from today). Where the pair has a surface the paths step its at-the-money term structure, as the ticket does by default: the Calibration sheet rebuilds each step’s vol from the quotes,
σk2​Δ=max(σATM​(tk​)2tk​−σATM​(tk−1​)2tk−1​, (41​σATM​(tk​))2Δ),(15)

and the Paths sheet steps Fk​=Fk−1​exp(−21​σk2​Δ+σk​Δ​Zk​); a digital asset’s steps run on the clock of its vol regimes (§9.3). The rest is the forward’s value on each path, the level bridged in logs a margin period earlier and the trade valued on it, the collateral, the exposures and the waterfall, in cells. Two ties are tested: the cells against the engine under each margin preset on five valuation dates, with a surface (97 to 101 checks, by the number of steps) and without one (79 to 82), and the engine’s figures against POST /api/xva/currency for the same forward, paths and seed, to the cent. Until this version the books priced a six-month forward from illustrative inputs at one vol on monthly steps, where a six-month ticket runs weekly ones: they held the engine’s arithmetic, not a ticket’s run. Not in the book: a ticket’s fees; wrong-way risk as a default intensity tied to the asset (§10; the book has the multiplier alone, at one); the capital of a Group 2b digital asset (the book’s asset is Group 2a); the two older capital models, which are in the cells and are not checked; a margin period of a grid step or longer.

Replication of an option’s run (version 1.46). The workbooks xva\_fx\_option and xva\_crypto\_option are the run of an option ticket’s XVA tab in its flat-vol mode, for a bought European call struck at the forward, eighteen months: on EUR 10m against USD, and on 10 BTC cash-settled in USD. One vol, the surface’s at the option’s expiry and strike (rebuilt on the Calibration sheet, the smile’s fixed point iteration by iteration), drives every path and values the option on every path. On each path the forward to settlement Ft​ implies the spot St​=Ft​e−(rq​−rb​)(Ts​−t), with rb​=rq​−ln(F0​/S0​)/Ts​ the carry the forward implies, and before the expiry the option is
V(t)=±Ne−rq​τ[Fe​Φ(d1​)−KΦ(d2​)],Fe​=St​e(rq​−rb​)τ,τ=Te​−t,d1,2​=στ​ln(Fe​/K)±21​σ2τ​,(16)

a put by the same formula with the signs turned; at the last grid date, the settlement date, it is its payoff on the spot there. A margin period earlier it is the same closed form on the level bridged there, with the time left there; in the last step, which holds the expiry, the time left runs to the last grid date, the settlement date, where the paths fix the payoff, and not to the expiry a few days before it: the paths’ own approximation, stated above, and the book’s. A digital asset’s spot moves on the clock of its vol regimes (§9.3) and the option is still valued at the one vol on every path. The capital add-on is the class’s supervisory factor on the notional at spot times the option’s supervisory delta (CRE52.40: the Black delta of the strike at the class’s supervisory volatility, 15% for a currency pair and 120% for a digital asset), held along the grid. A bought option owes nothing on any path, so without collateral DVA and FBA are nil; under a credit support annex the residual takes both signs. Two ties are tested: the cells against the engine under each margin preset on five valuation dates, with a surface and without one (some ninety checks, the option’s value on single paths among them), and the engine’s figures against POST /api/xva/currency-option in the flat-vol mode, for the option as the ticket prices and books it, to the cent.

Not rebuilt. The ticket’s default mode steps the paths on the surface’s term structure and reads the smile at each path’s moneyness, the paths grouped into eight by their vol and each group valued at its mean vol: that mode has no workbook. Neither have the other styles (American, digital, barrier, double barrier, touch). A sold option is shown by turning the book’s Side cell and is not checked. As in the forward books, a ticket’s fees, wrong-way risk as a default intensity tied to the asset, the capital of a Group 2b digital asset and a margin period of a grid step or longer are not in the book, and the two older capital models are in its cells unchecked. The book is written for an expiry inside the grid’s last step, which an eighteen-month option’s is.

What the book showed. The run’s value today is Ne−rq​Te​[Fe​Φ(d1​)−KΦ(d2​)] with Fe​=S0​e(rq​−rb​)Te​: the forward and the discounting are read at the expiry. The ticket prices the same option on the forward to settlement, discounted from the settlement date (§13). The two differ by the carry and the discounting over the days between the expiry and the settlement: on the checks’ market the run’s value today is 0.09% below the ticket’s price for the EURUSD call (four days) with a surface saved and 0.10% below without one; for the digital asset’s (one day) it is 0.002% below without a surface and 0.007% above with one, the discounting outweighing the carry at a digital asset’s vol. The exposure, and so every charge, starts from the run’s figure; the NPV on the ticket is the ticket’s price. It is stated here and not changed.
Volatility regimes of a digital asset

A digital asset’s daily returns are not draws from one bell curve. Violent days come together and pass within two or three days, and under that the whole level of activity is higher for a couple of months and then lower. One volatility reads the moves over a margin period too small, which is where collateral and initial margin are measured. On a digital-asset ticket (since v1.15) the volatility of day d is
σd​=σfd​sd​,(17)

where σ is the volatility the ticket carries (the surface’s, or the desk’s) and f and s are two independent two-state Markov chains: f calm or stressed, s low or high. A chain with high-to-low ratio ρ and daily probabilities a of staying low and b of staying high spends a share p=(1−a)/(2−a−b) of its days high, and its two levels are
ℓlow​=(1−p+pρ2)−1/2,ℓhigh​=ρℓlow​,so that(1−p)ℓlow2​+pℓhigh2​=1.(18)
Each path starts in each state with its long-run share; today’s regime is not read.

The regimes change the clock and not the law given the clock. With Uj​ the average of fd2​sd2​ over the days of grid step j (the variance the step accumulated on the path, as a multiple of σj2​Δt), the level of §12 steps as
lnM(tj​)−lnM(tj−1​)=−21​σj2​ΔtUj​+σj​ΔtUj​​Zj​,E[Uj​]=1,(19)

with the same standard normals Zj​ a run on one volatility draws. Three things follow. M is still a martingale, so every forward starts at its own price. The variance expected to any date is σ2t, so today’s value of a forward or an option is unchanged and the volatility on the ticket means what it says. An option on the paths is still marked at the surface’s volatility, which is not what the regime paths pay on average: an option at the money pays less than its mark when the variance to expiry is uncertain, by about 3.6% one month from expiry, 1.2% at six months and 0.4% at two years. To that extent an option’s simulated value is not a martingale, and its exposure carries a bias of that size. And an uncollateralised ticket’s exposure, which is set by the spread of the level at each date, moves little: an exposure at the money is lower when the variance to a date is uncertain than when it is fixed at the same average, by 1 to 3% on tickets of a year or less. What changes most is the move over days and weeks. The value a margin period earlier is the bridge of §9 on the clock: the share Ω of the step’s variance that came before t−δ takes the place of the share w of its time, and the step’s variance is the path’s own, lnM(t−δ)∣⋅∼N(lnM(tj−1​)+ΩΔlnM,σj2​ΔtUj​Ω(1−Ω)). The bridge draws nothing more than it did.

The fit. The six parameters of an asset (a ratio and two probabilities per chain) are fitted by maximum likelihood, with Hamilton’s filter, to five years of public daily closes (backend/scripts/calibrate_vol_regimes.py; 1,826 returns to 11 November 2026). They are dated constants in pricing/vol_regimes.py; a refit is a reviewed change. The fast chain is calm or stressed, the slow one low or high; a ratio is the higher volatility over the lower, and the other columns are how long a spell in each state lasts on average. The chains are named by how long their high state lasts. SOL’s fast chain is calm for 37 days at a time, close to the spells of its slow chain, so its two chains are less clearly told apart than BTC’s or ETH’s.

Against one volatility the fast chain alone raises the log-likelihood by 164 to 190; the slow chain adds 36 to 41 more for three parameters. A regular chi-squared reference would put the 5% bar at about 4; the true bar is higher, because the slow chain’s two probabilities mean nothing when its ratio is one, but not by that much. The comparison is in-sample: there is no holdout, and no standard errors are reported for the parameters. blocks.html: The bands are wide: five years hold about 180 ten-day periods that do not overlap, and a 1st percentile of those is two observations. The tail figures alone would not tell the regimes from a Gaussian; the daily likelihood does. The mean move beyond the percentile is still smaller in the fit than in the history (for BTC over ten days −27.4% against −31.3%, a Gaussian’s being −22.7%): the worst weeks of the five years are worse than two chains make them.

What was tried and not kept, on the same closes. Merton’s jump-diffusion by maximum likelihood puts about 230 jumps a year on BTC, each of 3%: the day-to-day clustering read as jumps. Being independent from day to day they average out, and the ten-day tail comes out within a point of a Gaussian’s. The fast chain alone fits the days better than jumps do but its stress is over in two or three days, and its ten-day tail is still thin (−21.3% for BTC).

What it does to a ticket. Measured on forwards of about one million of notional at 55, 70 and 95% volatility, six months and two years, 40,000 paths, against the same run on one volatility: uncollateralised, CVA and FCA fall by up to 3% on tickets of a year or less and the total moves by about 1% or less; under a bilateral or an on-chain CSA the margin at the first date rises 7 to 13% (what is called 9 to 13%, what is posted 7 to 11%), MVA with it by 2 to 10% on BTC and ETH, the exposure left beyond the margin by more (CVA 15 to 45% higher, on figures that are small), and KVA falls 4 to 13% on BTC and ETH, where the larger margin lowers the SA-CCR multiplier; SOL’s, a Group 2b asset with no multiplier, does not move. The total moves by 1.5 to 6% on BTC and ETH and within about 1% either way on SOL, whose capital charge dominates. The engine’s margin estimate with the regimes on agrees to sampling, at every date, with a simulation written apart from it that redraws both chains and steps the level every day (tests/test_vol_regimes.py).

The backtest. Does the simulated level cover what the level did? After the Basel Committee’s sound practices for backtesting counterparty credit risk models (December 2010): on every day of the five years (the first 90 are warm-up) the model is given a volatility and asked for the 1st, 5th, 95th and 99th percentile of the log move over the next 5, 10, 14, 30 and 91 days, and the move that followed is counted as beyond each or not. The volatility given is the realised volatility of the 90 days before, since the history of the implied volatilities a ticket carries is not held; the drift is the martingale’s. Days overlap and the volatility is itself an estimate, so a binomial band would be wrong: the same procedure is run on 500 histories simulated from the model itself, and the band is where 95% of those counts fall. A forward’s value is monotone in the level, so the level’s percentile is the trade’s: the 14-day rows test the initial margin (the 99th percentile over the margin period, each way).

The table is the share of days, in per cent of about 1,720, on which the 14-day move went beyond the model’s percentile, with the model’s own band in brackets; bold is outside the band. Over the five horizons and four percentiles (60 cells) one volatility is outside its band in 17 (8 on BTC, 7 on SOL, 2 on ETH, all but one at 5 to 30 days) and the regimes in 1: BTC’s 91-day move above the 95th percentile, 16.3% of days against a band that ends at 16.2%, a coin that rose forecast with the martingale’s drift. This run is in sample for the regimes, whose parameters were fitted to the same five years. A 95% band leaves about 3 of 60 outside when the model is true; the cells are not independent, and neither are the three coins, which share one market. With the regimes refitted on the first three years and tested on the two after, they are outside in none of the 60; nor is one volatility, for those two years were quieter and 720 days cannot tell the two apart. Run on histories of known law (forty of five years, at ten days), the procedure puts a model given its own histories outside the band in 4% of cells for one volatility and 6% for the regimes, and catches one volatility in a tail, on histories the regimes made, in 25 of the 40.

What the backtest is not. The volatility in it is realised, not the implied volatility of a ticket. The up side is less comfortable than the down side: BTC’s 14-day move went above the 99th percentile on 2.96% of days, at the very edge of the band, and SOL’s on 2.44%; the model is close to symmetric in logs and these coins’ rallies were not. That percentile is the margin the desk calls on a position worth more to it when the coin rises (a forward bought, a call bought): the side on which the margin was exceeded most often, inside the band but not by much. The bands are wide, from about 0.2 to 3% at the 1st percentile, and their lower edge is at or near zero: the test rejects a model whose tails are too thin; it does not certify a good one, and it cannot reject one whose tails are too wide (BTC’s 91-day move never went below the regimes’ 1st percentile). The realised volatility of the last 90 days already carries the slow regime of the moment, and the regimes add their slow variation on top of it, so in a high-volatility spell the forecast may lean wide; this was not measured. It tests the level and not a portfolio: an option’s exposure also depends on the volatility the paths carry, which is not backtested. The margin period of ten business days is 10/250 of a year, 14.6 days on the regimes’ clock of 365; the test’s 14 days are a little short of it.

Limits. Two states a chain is a coarse picture of volatility; the stress the chains produce is milder than the worst the history has. The spells are of days and of months: nothing here makes the level of volatility itself uncertain over years, so the uncertainty in the variance to a date falls with the tenor (its coefficient of variation is about a half at one month, a third at six months and a sixth at two years) and a ten-year ticket’s tails are close to a lognormal’s again: on long tickets the regimes understate. Default and the regimes are independent: a stressed state does not make default likelier, which understates wrong-way risk when stress and default come together. A barrier or a touch is watched on the grid dates of the regime paths and marked by a closed form that watches continuously at the surface’s volatility; the difference that was there before is carried over and has not been measured again on these paths. The closes the fit read are fetched, not kept in the repository: the table is reproduced by running the script, on whatever the source then returns. The parameters are fitted to spot returns and held fixed over the life of the trade, to ten years on the longest tickets. Today’s state is not inferred, though the last weeks’ returns say something about it: a ticket priced in a stressed month and one priced in a calm month start from the same mix. The volatility on the ticket is read as the average over the trade’s life. The regimes drive the level of a ticket’s XVA only: the counterparty-credit simulation of §15 and the market-risk history of §14 are unchanged, the first on one volatility per factor and the second on the history itself. A currency pair keeps one volatility.
Initial margin

Initial margin is one of two things. An amount the desk sets, in the trade’s currency, exchanged each way and held for the life of the trade. Or the engine’s own estimate from the simulated paths: at each grid date ti​, with Δi​=V(ti​)−V(ti​−δ) the change in the set’s value over the margin period (the lagged value of the bridge above) and Δˉi​ its mean across paths,
IMrecv​(ti​)=max(q0.99​(Δi​−Δˉi​),0),IMpost​(ti​)=max(q0.99​(Δˉi​−Δi​),0),(20)

the 99th percentile rise (the margin we call) and fall (the margin we post). The confidence is the one the margin rules for non-centrally cleared derivatives name (BCBS–IOSCO: a one-tailed 99 per cent interval over the margin horizon). The mean is removed because what every path does over the period (a scheduled payment, the passage of time) is not a risk. The estimate is at the model’s current volatility, not one calibrated to a period of stress, so it can read lower than a regulatory margin model; it is a cross-section of the paths at each date, not a margin recomputed on each path. On currency and digital-asset tickets the value a margin period earlier is exact (above), and against a simulation that draws the level at both dates, with no grid and no bridge, the estimate agrees to sampling error (about 1% at 200,000 paths; tests/test\_fx\_xva\_lag.py). Bridging between values, as those tickets did until v1.14 and as the rates ticket and the netting-set engine still do, keeps the variance of the move but is Gaussian where the value is lognormal: within about 1% at a currency’s volatility, and 9 to 18% low on the margin called at volatilities of 55 to 110%. Exposure beyond the margin is then the 1% tail of the model’s own move, so a margined CVA is small by construction: gap risk, jumps and a margin call that is not met are not in it. A leg of a package that settles is a payment, not a move, and is not margined. Received IM reduces exposure; posted IM is funded and drives MVA. Function model_im.
Rijeka does not compute ISDA SIMM. SIMM is ISDA’s licensed methodology and its risk weights are not in this engine. A firm with a SIMM licence enters its own figure as the amount.
Residual exposure
E+(t)=max(V(t)−C(t)−IMrecv​(t),0),E−(t)=min(V(t)−C(t)+IMpost​(t),0).(21)
Expected exposure EE(t)=E[E+(t)], expected negative exposure ENE(t)=E[E−(t)] and the 97.5% potential future exposure are reported per date.
Presets

rows: daily VM, 10-business-day margin period (the BCBS–IOSCO floor for non-cleared trades), initial margin, thresholds and MTA from the CSA.
atomic settlement: continuous VM, zero threshold and MTA, 5-business-day margin period (the cleared floor), initial margin over that shorter period.

blocks.html: The on-chain preset is the quantitative claim behind the confirmation layer: with continuous settlement the margin period halves, the initial margin estimate falls by about 1−1/2​≈29% (a diffusion’s move over half the period), and the SA-CCR maturity factor falls in the same proportion.
SA-CCR

For margined netting sets the maturity factor is MF=1.5max(δ,floor)/250​ and replacement cost RC=max(V−C,TH+MTA−NICA,0) with NICA the IM received; unmargined sets use MF=min(M,1)​ and RC=max(V,0). The interest-rate supervisory factor is 0.5% and α=1.4. Capital is 8% of risk-weighted exposure and feeds KVA.
The add-on of a currency or digital-asset ticket
A currency or digital-asset ticket takes the add-on of its own asset class (pricing/fx_xva.py, capital_inputs; pricing/sa_ccr.py).
A currency pair: the foreign-exchange class, supervisory factor 4% on the notional of the foreign leg in the domestic currency at spot, one hedging set per pair (CRE52.35, CRE52.72).

A Group 2a cryptoasset: SA-CCR with a cryptoasset class in the structure of the foreign-exchange class, a hedging set per pair, supervisory factor 32% and supervisory option volatility 120% (SCO60.98).
A Group 2b cryptoasset: exposure =α(RC+PFE) with the PFE 50% of the gross notional of each transaction, no hedging set and no multiplier (SCO60.99).
A forward enters at δ=±1 and an option at the supervisory delta of its strike (CRE52.40); the legs of one ticket net inside the hedging set, except under Group 2b.

A cryptoasset is Group 2b unless the bank has shown its supervisor the hedging recognition criteria of SCO60.55 (a regulated derivative or exchange-traded product, USD 10bn of average market capitalisation, USD 50m of trimmed mean daily volume, a year of price observations); the engine’s default is Group 2a for BTC and ETH and Group 2b otherwise, and the desk sets the group on the ticket. A style whose size is a payout enters at its payout: the rules name no notional for it, and that is this engine’s reading.

blocks.html: Default probabilities come from the credit triangle: hazard rate h=s/LGD for a flat or term-structured spread s, survival Q(t)=e−ht. With Di​=P(ti​), Δt the grid step and ΔQi​=Q(ti−1​)−Q(ti​),

CVAFCAKVA​=−LGDcp​i∑​EEi​ΔQicp​Qˉ​iown​Di​ωi​,=−i∑​siftp​EEi​Si​ΔtDi​,=−i∑​κKi​ΔtDi​,​DVAFBAMVA​=LGDown​i∑​∣ENEi​∣ΔQiown​Qˉ​icp​Di​,=i∑​max(siftp​−siown​,0)∣ENEi​∣Si​ΔtDi​,=−i∑​IMi​max(siftp​−π,0)ΔtDi​,​(22)(23)(24)​
ColVA=i∑​(VMipost​spost+VMirecv​srecv)ΔtDi​,(25)

with Qˉ​i​=21​(Q(ti−1​)+Q(ti​)) a party’s survival at the middle of step i. Each adjustment is signed as its effect on our value: a cost is negative and a benefit positive, and the total is their sum. FCA is the cost of funding what is owed to us and is not collateralised, FBA the benefit of funding where we owe, and the funding valuation adjustment is the two together, FVA=FCA+FBA; it is two of the components and is not added to the total a second time. (Until version 1.23 the cost alone was called FVA, here and on the screens, and these formulas were written as magnitudes.) Here ωi​ is an optional wrong-way-risk multiplier, κ the capital hurdle rate, Ki​ the SA-CCR capital on the exposure path with the trade’s remaining life read at the middle of step i (capital and margin are held through the step, so the step that ends on the maturity is charged like every other; until 0.27.0 the life was read at the step’s end, where it is zero, and a one-month trade on its two monthly steps was charged for one), and π a yield pick-up on posted collateral (tokenised collateral that earns a return reduces MVA). ColVA is the carry of the variation margin against cash at the OIS the discounting assumes: VMipost​ and VMirecv​ are the mean margin posted and held at step i (the two sides of C in §9), spost and srecv the carries over OIS of what each side is held in (§16); cash on both sides gives zero, so every figure that predates instruments is unchanged. The waterfall is reported gross and under the CSA, so the benefit of collateral is visible term by term.

The exposure is discounted on its own path (since version 1.35). Each charge above is an expectation of a discounted amount: in CVA, EEi​Di​ stands for E[D(ti​)V+(ti​)], what the desk is owed at ti​ discounted on the path it is owed on, and ∣ENEi​∣Di​ for E[D(ti​)V−(ti​)]; FCA and FBA read the same two, and ColVA the margin balances the same way. Where rates are simulated the engine computes E[D(ti​)V+(ti​)]=P(0,ti​)E[wi​V+(ti​)] with wi​=D(ti​)/P(0,ti​) the path’s own discounting over today’s curve’s, D(ti​)=1/A(ti​) on the account of §15; the expectation of wi​ is one at every date (the sample’s mean is within its sampling error of one, tested), and the engine sets the sample mean to one exactly, so that the sampling error of the paths’ own mean discount factor is not carried into a charge and an exposure that does not move with rates is charged as before. Until version 1.35 it took the product of the means, P(0,ti​)E[V+(ti​)], which is the same thing only where discounting and exposure are independent. They are not on a rates trade: a receive-fixed swap is owed most on the paths where rates have fallen, which are the paths discounted least, so the product of the means understates what it is owed and overstates what it owes, and a pay-fixed swap the other way; the difference grows with the life of the trade and with volatility. Two outside figures. (i) With the exposure read once a year, on the coupon dates, a swap’s unilateral CVA is LGD∑k​Swaptionkrec​ΔQk​ and its DVA the payer swaptions’: on a six-year receive-fixed swap at par, under the same Hull–White parameters, curve and survival curves, the waterfall stood over four seeds of 40,000 paths between −0.41 and +0.04% of QuantLib’s Jamshidian strip on CVA and between −0.70 and +0.47% on DVA (one seed carries about half a per cent of sampling error); with the product of the means it stood between −2.16 and −2.58% and between +1.58 and +2.80%, and on the same paths, where that error cancels, 2.2% lower on CVA and 2.3% higher on DVA at every seed (two rows of the reference suite, §18, and a test of that difference; the model validator’s own paths, a five-year swap on a flat curve at 400,000 paths: 1.8% each way). (ii) ORE, the Open Source Risk Engine (version 1.8.17, an exposure and XVA engine built on QuantLib), on a five-year receive-fixed overnight swap of 10 million with the same curve, dates, Hull–White parameters and survival curves, on a weekly grid: expected exposure within 1% at every date read, unilateral CVA 0.24% and DVA 0.17% below ORE’s; with the product of the means CVA stood 2.3% below and DVA 1.9% above (17 November 2026; run by hand, not on every commit). On the monthly grid the engine uses, the same comparison stands at 0.8% and 1.0%: interest inside a monthly step accrues at the rate known when the step begins (§15), and ORE fills a step with the rate at its end; each is about half of that from the weekly figure, in opposite directions. What this does not do. A currency or digital-asset ticket simulates no rates, so its discounting is today’s curve on every path and nothing changes. A request that carries no trade is answered with the generic swap, whose paths carry no account: it stays on the product of the means, and so does the xva\_rates workbook that rebuilds it. A netting set in several currencies is discounted on the account of the curve its values are reported on. KVA and MVA are sums of expected capital and expected margin and are discounted on today’s curve as before. The exposure profiles shown (EE, ENE, PFE) are undiscounted values at the grid dates, so CVA can no longer be read off the chart by multiplying by a discount factor. FCA, FBA and ColVA read the same weighted exposures and have no outside figure of their own; a margined set, a set in several currencies and wrong-way risk together with the weight have none either. The first XVA P&L and the first counterparty report after the release carry the change as if the market had moved (§11): a stored report is not restated.

First to default. The counterparty’s default costs the desk only if the desk has not defaulted before it, and the desk’s own default is a gain to it only if the counterparty has not defaulted before. With τcp​ and τown​ the two default times and V the value of the set to the desk,
CVA=−LGDcp​E[1{τcp​≤T, τcp​<τown​}D(τcp​)V+(τcp​)],DVA=LGDown​E[1{τown​≤T, τown​<τcp​}D(τown​)V−(τown​)].(26)

The two defaults are taken to be independent of each other (given the market path), so the condition that the other party has not defaulted first is the other party’s survival at the moment of default: CVA=−LGDcp​∫0T​EE(t)D(t)Qown(t)(−dQcp(t)), and DVA with the parties exchanged. On the grid the default probability of a step is ΔQi​ and the other party’s survival is read at the middle of the step, Qˉ​i​, the rule Si​ below already follows. With constant intensities λcp​,λown​ the exact probability that the counterparty defaults in a step before the desk is Qi−1cp​Qi−1own​λcp​+λown​λcp​​(1−e−(λcp​+λown​)Δt); ΔQicp​Qˉ​iown​ is that to second order in the step. Over five years on a monthly grid the two were measured to agree to 10−7 at spreads of 250 and 120 bp, 2×10−6 at 1,200 and 900 bp and 9×10−5 with one party at 4,000 bp, and to 7×10−6 with the two loss rates unequal (tests/test\_first\_to\_default.py, which bounds each a little above its measurement). The model validator derived both figures again from the definition, on paths of the validator’s own, by the exact step probability and by simulating the two default times (30 million draws): the engine stood within 10−7 of the exact figure at 85 and 42 bp and 2×10−5 at 1,500 and 1,000 bp, and the simulation within its sampling error of both (17 November 2026). That the two first-to-default probabilities and the chance both survive sum to one is an identity of the midpoint rule and is not evidence for it. The treatment is that of Brigo and Capponi (Bilateral counterparty risk valuation with stochastic dynamical models and application to credit default swaps, 2008) and of Gregory (The xVA Challenge, bilateral CVA); in Burgard and Kjaer the same weight follows from discounting at r+λown​+λcp​. Until version 1.31 neither figure carried the weight: each party was charged as if the other could not default before it (unilateral CVA and DVA). Those two figures are still computed and are in every answer (unilateral), for a reader who compares with a system that quotes them. What this does not do: the two defaults have no dependence on each other beyond what the market path gives them (where both are tied to the asset they are correlated through it, and only through it), and the two never default at the same instant; the set is closed out at its risk-free value, with no replacement cost that looks at the survivor’s credit (the assumption under which Burgard and Kjaer’s discounting gives this weight); the weight is read at the date of the default and not at the close-out, so a survivor that defaults inside the margin period of risk of a collateralised set is not counted; and the capital charge for CVA risk (§16) is unilateral by rule and does not see the weight.

The funding adjustment: the cost, the benefit, and why the benefit is on the basis. Here siftp​ is the desk’s funding spread over OIS over step i, siown​ its own credit spread over the same step, and Si​=21​(Qi−1cp​Qi−1own​+Qicp​Qiown​) the chance that neither party has defaulted, read at the middle of the step. The cost and the benefit are kept as two figures, and they are not symmetric.

Why. A desk’s funding spread is its own credit spread plus a basis: what its funding costs beyond its credit (liquidity). On what the desk owes, DVA already credits it with its own credit spread: LGDown​ΔQiown​ is that spread over the step, times the desk’s survival. A funding benefit at the whole funding spread on the same exposure would count the credit part a second time. That a naive funding adjustment beside CVA and DVA counts twice what can be realised once is the point of Morini and Prampolini (Risky Funding: A Unified Framework for Counterparty and Liquidity Charges) and of Burgard and Kjaer (In the Balance; Funding Strategies, Funding Costs); the rule used here is motivated by those papers and is this engine’s own, not a formula taken from them. FBA is charged on the basis alone, max(siftp​−siown​,0), step by step. A desk that funds at its own credit spread has no funding benefit beyond its DVA. Where its stated funding spread is below its credit spread the basis is zero, not a negative benefit; DVA is not capped at the funding spread, so on those steps the desk is credited with more than it says it pays for funds. The cost is not reduced in the same way: on what is owed to the desk the credit is the counterparty’s, which is CVA, and the desk still funds the whole amount at its whole funding spread.

How: one reading of a spread curve. A spread quoted for a tenor covers the whole of (0,t): the credit triangle reads a CDS curve so, Q(t)=e−s(t)t/LGD, and what DVA charges over a step is therefore the forward spread of that step, siown​=LGDown​ln(Qi−1own​/Qiown​)/Δt=(s(ti​)ti​−s(ti−1​)ti−1​)/Δt. The funding curve is read the same way, siftp​=(sftp(ti​)ti​−sftp(ti−1​)ti−1​)/Δt floored at zero, in FCA, in FBA and in MVA, so that the two spreads compared in the basis are spreads of the same step and DVA and FBA together credit the funding spread of each step once. (A first form of this version compared the tenor’s own spreads, sftp(ti​)−sown(ti​): on a rising own-credit curve DVA charges more than sown(ti​), and the two together stood 10 to 18% above the funding spread on the default curves; found by the model validator before release.) A flat spread is itself at every step. Between two quoted tenors the spread is interpolated in a straight line, as the credit triangle has always read a CDS curve, so the forward spread is not flat between tenors and steps at each one: on the default funding curve (42 to 62 bp from one year to ten) the forward runs from 42 to 75 bp and steps by up to 5 bp at a tenor, and beyond the last tenor, where the spread is held, it falls back to that spread. With forwards held flat between tenors instead, the funding cost of a swap-like exposure is 0.6 to 0.8% larger at five years and 0.4% at ten, and DVA 0.07% smaller (the model validator’s figures and the author’s, 17 November 2026): a limitation of the interpolation, stated and not mended, because changing it would move CVA and DVA as well. An own-credit curve under which no survival is left is read at the tenor’s own spread. With the defaults a desk is shown, the term basis to five years is 55−48=7 bp, and the XVA tab prints that figure beside the assumptions as the average basis over five years; a trade of another length is charged on its own steps. Until version 1.30 the benefit was a fixed share (55%) of the funding spread whatever the desk’s own spread was, a figure that was a default and was not derived; it has been removed.

What is and is not weighted by survival. Funding is paid and earned only while the trade is alive, so FCA and FBA carry Si​; the curves are the ones the market gives (default independent of the market in this weight, also where CVA and DVA carry wrong-way risk). CVA and DVA carry the other party’s survival (first to default, above), so the own-credit part of the benefit, which is in DVA, and the basis part, which is in FBA, are weighted alike: LGDown​ΔQiown​Qˉ​icp​ is the desk’s own spread over the step times the chance both parties are alive, to second order, and DVA and FBA together are the funding spread of each step credited once under Si​ (to 10−4 on a five-year case with flat spreads of 42, 85 and 55 bp for the desk, the counterparty and funding; until version 1.31 the two stood 4.8 to 4.9% above it, because DVA carried the desk’s survival alone). KVA and MVA are not weighted by survival. Where the desk’s own default is tied to the asset the identity is one of the independent figures, not of the charge: DVA with the desk’s default on its curve, plus FBA, is the funding spread credited once, and the link’s effect on DVA stands on top of it, because FBA reads the curves and does not see the link (on a three-year bought forward under water with the desk’s intensity trebling when the asset halves, DVA is 87% above its independent figure and DVA plus FBA 66% above the funding spread credited once; the model validator’s case, 17 November 2026). Survival never rises along a curve: where a steeply inverted curve would have it rise it is held where it stood, in CVA, DVA and the weight alike, so such a step is charged no default and the default probabilities of all the steps sum to one less the lowest survival. No adjustment’s sign is set at the end of a run; each is the sum of its steps with the sign those steps have. A swap whose curve is not stored is not simulated on a stand-in: the run is refused and says which curve is missing. Whether a funding adjustment belongs in a price at all is argued in the literature; the engine reports the components and takes no side, and which of them enter the signed P&L is the firm’s policy (§11).

Currency and digital-asset tickets: the grid, and the exposure a charge reads. A ticket of a year or less (up to 372 days) is stepped weekly, a longer one monthly. At step i CVA, DVA, FCA and FBA read not EEi​ but the exposure averaged across the step, 21​(EEi−1​+EEi​) (the same for ENE, and path by path where wrong-way risk links default to the level), with EE0​ today’s exposure: today’s value less the collateral that value calls, with the first date’s initial margin. The exposure of a forward grows like t​; read at each step’s end on two or three monthly steps it overstated the charge. Measured on a digital-asset forward dealt at fair value, 55% volatility, 20,000 paths, against daily steps: CVA was 31% high at one month, 23% at three, 8% at six and 9% at a year uncollateralised, and 23%, 6%, 3% and 2% under a ten-day margin period. On weekly steps with the averaged exposure it is within 4% of daily steps at every one of those tenors, both ways. Against continuous time, by closed form on one volatility (the expected exposure of a forward dealt at K is a call’s undiscounted value, integrated against the default density), the old rule read 28% high at one month and 20% at three, and the engine now reads 2.7% and 1.7% low: the averaged rule is a trapezoid, which on a profile that grows like t​ reads low by 2.6% at one month, 0.7% at three and 0.1% at a year. A step starts from the set less what was paid on that date, so a settled leg of a package is not charged for one more step. The profiles shown (EE, ENE, PFE) are the values at the grid dates; the replacement cost in KVA, the margin in MVA and ColVA are read at each step’s end. A swap’s waterfall and the netting-set engine of §15 keep monthly steps and the exposure at each step’s end: the same measurement has not been made there. Known limitations: the first step’s average starts from an exposure built on today’s value alone; a margined KVA still reads about 4% below daily steps on a six-month ticket and MVA 1% above; the replication workbook runs monthly steps (its arithmetic is the grid’s own; that the grids agree is a test on the engine); a barrier is still watched only at the grid dates.

The charge on the ticket. Every ticket’s XVA tab carries, under the trade’s stand-alone number, the incremental charge: the counterparty’s netting set valued on the credit engine’s risk-neutral paths (§15) with the trade and without it, the same paths for both runs, the difference per component. That is the number a desk quotes; the stand-alone figure is the trade on its own under a chosen CSA preset. An opened or freshly booked trade shows the marginal form, the set with and without it. The route is POST /api/xva/incremental; the hypothetical trade is the ticket’s booking body with its legs completed as the booking route would store them, so what is charged is what would be booked. Capital in the set (since version 1.36): the set’s KVA is charged on its SA-CCR rows, each trade in its own asset class and hedging set (§16), the rows the capital report charges on. Until then the counterparty run took the single-factor interest-rate add-on on the set’s gross notional whatever the set held: a six-month EURUSD forward of 10 million was charged −78 in the set against some −1,400 on its ticket, and a forward on ten bitcoin nothing against some −1,100. With the rows, on one day’s market and 4,000 paths, the two stand at −1,388 against −1,409 and −1,030 against −1,109. By hand from the Basel text (CRE52: supervisory factor 4%, the unmargined maturity factor on the remaining life at the middle of each step, α=1.4, no replacement cost) a six-month forward of 11.6 million dollars is charged −1,465.16, and the engine gives that figure to nine digits (the model validator’s calculation, now tests/test\_ccr.py). Every set’s capital charge can change, not only a forward’s: a swap alone in a set, and two swaps the same way, are unchanged to the cent; a swaption alone is charged −8,014 where it was −13,214, because it enters at its supervisory delta and not at its whole notional; a swap and its mirror are charged nothing where they were charged −14,511 on their gross notional, because they offset in one hedging set. What the mapping to rows had to assume (a cryptoasset run in the class of Group 2a where its ticket’s default is Group 2b, a stand-in rate, a trade it could not map) is in the answer (capital\_notes), and a set whose rows cannot be built is charged as before and says so. Where a ticket and its set still differ, measured. A swap: within 0.2% (§9). A currency or digital-asset forward: the ticket steps weekly and reads the exposure averaged across each step; the set steps monthly and reads each step’s end, so a trade stands in the set until the first monthly date after it has gone. In closed form (a driftless lognormal asset at 8% volatility, a flat hazard, no discounting, against a grid of 20,000 steps), a forward that settles on a grid date is charged, on the set’s reading, 10.6% more CVA at six months, 2.9% at two years and 1.2% at five; on the ticket’s, 0.2% less at six months and 0.03% at two years; the average of each monthly step would be 2.0% and 0.3% less. A trade that settles in the middle of a step is charged about right by the set and one that settles just before a grid date too little. On the stack’s market, where the two runs also read volatility differently, the set’s CVA of a six-month EURUSD forward stood 8% above the ticket’s and of a two-year forward 1%. DVA is further apart where the two runs draw the asset differently: a digital asset’s ticket draws volatility regimes (§9) and the set one lognormal volatility (18% on the six-month bitcoin forward), and KVA within 2 to 7% for the grid. Reading each step’s average on the monthly grid is not the mend: against ORE it understates a five-year swap’s CVA by 2%, because a coupon is taken out up to a month before it is paid, where the step’s end is 0.3% off. The mend is to carry each payment to its own date inside the step; it is not built. A payment under margin (since version 1.36): where the charges are read on a step’s average (a currency or digital-asset ticket, a package), a leg that settles on the step’s date leaves the set at the step’s start, and under a margin agreement its collateral leaves with it: a settlement is a payment and not a move, so it is neither margined nor left standing as collateral, or as a shortfall, for the step.
Wrong-way risk

On a currency or digital-asset ticket a party’s default can be tied to the asset, in the manner of Hull and White (2012): an intensity that is a function of a simulated variable, with a time-dependent level calibrated to the credit curve. The variable (the asset against its forward, not the value of the portfolio) and the form (exponential) are this engine’s, so the direction is the desk’s input and is not derived from the trade. On path p at grid date ti​, with Mi​(p) the driver (the asset’s forward to settlement over that forward today),
hi​(p)=ci​Mi​(p)b,qi​(p)=qi−1​(p)e−hi​(p)Δt,Ep​[qi​(p)]=Q(ti​),(27)
where ci​ is solved date by date so that the mean survival is the credit curve’s: the curve is repriced exactly and b only moves default probability between paths. Then
CVA=−LGDcp​i∑​Ep​[Ei+​(p)(qi−1cp​(p)−qicp​(p))21​(qi−1own​(p)+qiown​(p))]Di​,(28)

and DVA likewise with the parties exchanged. A party that is not tied to the asset has the curve’s survival on every path, qi​(p)=Q(ti​). Because a tied party’s survival is also the weight on the other party’s default, a link on one party moves both figures: the one whose default is tied, by the link itself, and the other a little, through the weight (a counterparty that is likelier to have defaulted on the paths where the desk owes takes some of the desk’s DVA away; 0.6% of DVA and 0.3% of CVA in the two cases the tests pin). The independent figure the answer carries for a tied party is its charge with its default on the curve and the other party as it is, so what stands between the two is that party’s link alone, also when both are tied; a party that is not tied has no such figure. The link’s weight was not checked against an outside calculation: the tests state it by hand as the engine does, and check what must follow from the definition (a variable that is the same on every path ties nothing; with a level exposure one link moves neither charge; two links in the same direction make both charges smaller, in opposite directions larger). The desk’s input is the multiple k the intensity takes when the asset halves against its forward, b=−log2​k; k=1 is independence and is the calculation above, number for number. The answer carries both figures. The multiple is the desk’s judgement of the counterparty and is not calibrated; one constant link per party; funding, capital and margin terms do not see it. Functions hazard_beta, path_survival.
A package of legs as one netting set

A ticket with several legs on one pair (a strip, a collar, a forward with an option) is simulated as one set (pricing/fx_xva.py, package_xva). Every forward of the pair is its own forward today times one driftless lognormal driver, Fj​(t)=Fj​(0)Mt​: one factor, carry deterministic, so each leg starts at its own price and the legs move together. A forward leg is marked ±N(Fj​(t)−K)D(t,Tj​) and an option leg is valued in its style’s closed form; a leg stays to the first grid date at or after its settlement and is nothing after. The summed paths go through the same waterfall, so exposure nets path by path before any charge is taken, the initial margin estimate follows the legs as they settle, and the add-on is the one above on the legs together. A package of one leg is that leg’s own run, draw for draw. One factor means the shape of the forward curve or of the vol term structure moving is not simulated.

blocks.html: Daily P&L is attributed by sequential full revaluation: from yesterday’s mark on yesterday’s market the valuation is moved one thing at a time, in a fixed order (carry, cash, each curve tenor bucket by bucket, FX spot and points), each step’s change a row, and what is left between the last step and today’s mark on today’s market is a residual row, shown and never spread. An amendment in the window is one step, NPV(new terms,m1​)−NPV(old terms,m1​), after the market steps run on the old terms. The rows sum to the change in mark plus cash by construction.

Cash counts the flows that left the mark, those paid in [d0​,d1​): the pricer keeps a flow in the value on its payment date, so a coupon paying today is cash tomorrow (before November 2026 the window was (d0​,d1​] and a payment date’s P&L counted the coupon twice, reversed the next day).
A volatility surface the trade is valued on (an FX option’s) is moved after spot and points, bucket by bucket, as a vol step; swaption and cap vols have no step yet and land in the residual.

Booked European swaptions are valued as options in P&L, VaR, stress and the ladder (Bachelier at the day’s nearest ATM grid vol; expiry, strike, payer or receiver and bought or sold from the booked terms, the fixed leg’s forward start and rate when the terms are older); until November 2026 they were valued as their underlying swap.
Independent price verification

Module: backend/ipv; full description in docs/ipv.md. The controller verifies the inputs the book is priced on, not the trades: the list is the union over the trades in scope of the curves, funding levels, surfaces and spots they read (pnl.valuation.trade_curves), and each input is laddered per pillar through the production pricers, one quote moved by one unit (1bp of a rate, 1bp of normal vol, one vol point, 1% of spot) and the dependent trades repriced.

A pillar is a tenor, a swaption point (expiry×tenor) or an FX point (tenor,ATM/RR/BF); against an independent mark it carries a gap in the input’s unit, a status against the firm’s tolerance rule (the most specific rule wins) and a materiality flag (∣s∣⋅tol against the threshold).

An override is a market-data event with author and reason; its first-order P&L is sΔ and the full revaluation on the overridden market gives the residual as second order. Official P&L = flash + first order + second order + the day’s netted XVA reserve change, signed by the controller once every input is settled and every trade valued; the trading P&L shows the flash beside it.
