blocks.html: FX spot, forwards and non-deliverable forwards on a currency pair, and forwards on BTC, ETH or SOL against USD, are one product priced by covered interest parity (cash-and-carry): borrow the quote currency, buy the base today and lend it, so the forward must repay the quote-currency interest. Each currency discounts off its own overnight-index curve (USD SOFR, EUR €STR, GBP SONIA, JPY TONAR, CHF SARON, AUD AONIA, CAD CORRA); a digital asset discounts at its funding rate rc​ (lending or staking yield, continuously compounded).

With spot S in quote per base, Pq​(T) the quote-currency discount factor and Pb​(T) the base-currency one, and ts​ the spot date (for a USD pair two business days counted in the other currency’s centre, then the first day open in both, so a USD holiday on T+1 is ignored; one business day for USDCAD; the valuation date itself for a digital asset, whose quoted spot settles at once),
F=SPq​(T)/Pq​(ts​)Pb​(T)/Pb​(ts​)​,NPVq​=±Nb​(F−K)Pq​(T);(29)
quoted forward points are measured from the spot date.

A tenor’s value date is the spot date plus the tenor: weeks as calendar days, months keeping the day of the month, the end-of-month rule when the spot date is the last business day of its month, rolled modified following on the joint calendar of the two currencies; a digital asset’s tenor counts from the trade date and its USD cash settles on the first New York business day on or after it. The calendars (New York, TARGET from the ECB’s rule, London, Zurich, Sydney, Toronto, Tokyo) reproduce QuantLib’s over three years (tests/reference/test_ref_calendars.py; until 9 November 2026 five of them lacked their regional days, so a USDCHF spot date could fall on Good Friday). (Before November 2026 the spot was applied from the valuation date, dropping the carry over the spot lag: 5.6 pips on a six-month USDJPY from a Friday.)

Non-deliverable forwards. An NDF pays one net amount against a fixing X of the pair on its fixing date Tf​, on or before its settlement date T: in the quote currency ±Nb​(X−K), or, when its record settles in the base currency, the same amount converted at the fixing, ±Nb​(X−K)/X. The fixing of a currency pair is its spot rate, and a spot rate published on Tf​ is the price for delivery on that day’s spot date D. A ticket’s fixing date is the latest business day of both currencies whose spot date is on or before the settlement date (two business days before it on most pairs, one on USDCAD), so D=T: the rate fixed is the rate for delivery on the settlement date, its expectation is the forward F(T), and Nb​(1−K/X) of the base currency delivered on T is worth Nb​(X−K) of the quote currency on T at that very rate. The NDF is then worth exactly what the deliverable forward is, in either settlement currency:
NPVq​=±Nb​(F(T)−K)Pq​(T).(30)
A record that fixes earlier, so that D<T, is read at the forward for delivery on D, and the amount is carried from D to T on the curve of the currency it is paid in:
NPVq​=±Nb​(F(D)−K)Pq​(T)(31)
paid in the quote currency, and
NPVq​=±Nb​(F(D)−K)Pq​(D)Pb​(D)Pb​(T)​(32)

paid in the base currency. Both take the expectation of the rate fixed as F(D) although the amount is paid on T, and the second takes the base curve’s forward discount factor from D to T as known: the covariance of the rate with the discounting over those days is left out. A record that fixes later than the usual day, so that the rate fixed would deliver after the settlement date (a fixing on the eve of the settlement date, or on it, as every ticket before version 0.39.0 of the engine wrote), is read at the settlement date, as the deliverable forward: the carry of the days between, at most the spot lag, is left out (about four pips on a USDJPY fixed the day before it settles). A digital asset’s quoted spot settles at once, so there D=Tf​. (The first build of this, on 14 November 2026, read a currency NDF at the fixing date itself, two days of carry short of the deliverable forward; the model validation of that day found it before it shipped.)

From the fixing date the trade is that one amount (settlement/rule.py, the rule a digital asset’s forward settles by). It settles on the fixing of the source its record names and on no other. No public feed stores a currency fixing: the dealers’ benchmark is licensed, and the European Central Bank asks that its reference rates not be used to settle transactions; a desk enters the fixing of the benchmark it is licensed for, and until one is stored the amount is on the stored spot of the fixing date and marked provisional (on the fixing day itself that spot may still be restated, while the sensitivities reported are those of a fixed amount). An amount in the quote currency is discounted from the settlement date. An amount in the base currency is that many units of the base currency delivered on the settlement date, valued as a forward on them at a contract rate of zero, so its value in the quote currency still moves with spot and with both curves until it is paid; at the fixing the two agree. The record decides the currency: tickets before version 0.39.0 of the engine wrote USD on every pair and the settlement date as the fixing date, so an older USDJPY settles in dollars and an older cross, which names neither of its two currencies, in its quote currency, and both are valued as the deliverable forward as they always were. Only the G10 pairs are offered: the fixing lags and calendars of the emerging-market NDF currencies are not modelled. The exposure paths of an XVA run still carry the level to the settlement date.

When a pair carries a quoted forward curve (forward points by tenor, saved like any other snapshot: a feed’s, manual or import), the outright at a date is spot plus the points interpolated linearly in time, and the difference to the parity forward is reported as the cross-currency basis; the account chooses, in configuration, whether forwards are priced off quoted points or implied from the two curves, and every quote states which it used.
Beyond the last quoted tenor TL​ nothing is held flat. What the last quote shows over parity is read as a rate and carried on:
b=tL​1​lnFpar(TL​)S+pL​​,F(T)=Fpar(T)ebt,T>TL​,(33)
with t in years from the spot date (ACT/365), pL​ the last quoted points in price units and Fpar the parity forward of the two curves.

On a currency pair b is the cross-currency basis at the last quote; on a digital asset it is the futures basis, and holding it flat holds the asset’s implied rate rc​−b flat from the last quote on. Until v1.13 the last points were held, which made a forward beyond the last tenor blind to the carry between the two dates.

Every price names the kind of forward it used: quoted (the date is a quoted tenor), interpolated (between two, linear in time as above) or implied (beyond the last, by the rule above, or parity alone when the pair has no points), with the method in words. The forwards page shows the same on each tenor to ten years, and a tenor can be switched off there: its points stay on the row and its date is priced like any unquoted one. A tenor a venue feed fills beyond the venue’s last listed expiry, by this same rule applied in the feed, prices as a pillar and is reported as implied.

Known limitations: one number read off the last quote stands in for the whole term structure of the basis beyond it, with no band of uncertainty; that number is what is left over against the parity of the two curves, so an error in a curve is inside it and is carried on; while the points are held a parallel move of either curve leaves a forward beyond the quotes where it was, as it leaves one inside them; a date within seven days of a quoted tenor’s round day count is called that tenor (a two-year ticket settles two calendar years from spot, a few days past 730); nothing trades that far out on a digital asset, so the forward there is a model’s and is marked so; inside the quoted tenors points are still linear in time; a digital asset’s option stops at its last vol tenor (two years) while its forward goes to ten.
For a digital asset against USD this reads
F=SPUSD​(T)e−rc​T​=Se(rUSD​−rc​)T,NPV=(F−K)NPUSD​(T).(34)
A non-deliverable European option is priced with Black-76 on that forward with lognormal volatility σ:
C=PUSD​(T)[FΦ(d1​)−KΦ(d2​)],d1,2​=σT​ln(F/K)±21​σ2T​,(35)
with the put from parity.

Settlement is in cash against a named settlement price source on a valuation date and time, and the canonical record carries exactly the fields the ISDA Digital Asset Derivatives Definitions name: digital asset, notional amount, strike or forward price and its currency, option type and exercise style, valuation and settlement dates, settlement currency and price source, premium amount, currency and payment date.

Status. Implemented in the engine (pricing/currency_forward.py, with pricing/crypto_forward.py as the digital-asset case), priced from parameters and from booked trades on G10 pairs and BTC, ETH, SOL; spot from public reference rates (ECB) and a public exchange feed, the funding rate a desk input; the Excel replications rebuild the FX and the digital-asset forward cell by cell with the engine’s NPV, spot delta (FX01, CRY01) and rate sensitivities (IR01; CRYBASIS01 on a digital asset, with the screens’ sign) beside the formulas. The canonical on-chain record carries an FX product (pair, both notionals, rate, value date, settlement type, NDF fixing fields) beside the digital-asset one.

Replication (version 1.45). The workbook fx\_forward is the EURUSD forward as the ticket opens it: settling three months after the pair’s spot date, the carry running from the spot date (τ) and the discounting from the settlement date to today (t), F=Se−rb​τPq​(0,spot)/Pq​(0,T) and the value N(F−K)Pq​(0,T). Its formula rows are evaluated outside Excel against the engine: the forward to twelve digits, the value and the three sensitivities to nine. Until this version the book carried from the valuation date and took its settlement date three calendar months from it, and its forward stood about 1.6 pips from the ticket’s. The digital-asset book crypto\_ndf is carried from the valuation date, as the asset’s spot settles at once.

Options on the digital assets are the FX option of §13 with the funding rate as the base rate, cash-settled against the settlement price source the day after expiry; the trade window prices and books them in every style (2 November 2026). A validation note: the first workbook had the discount-factor ratio inverted (forward below spot at positive USD rates); the engine’s parity test caught it and both were corrected on 28 October 2026.

sections.title: FX options
sections.module: Module: pricing/fx_option.py, pricing/fx_vol.py; route POST /api/currency/option/price; booked valuation in pnl/valuation.py, exposure in ccr/options.py, record in chain/canonical.py.

blocks.html: A European option on a currency pair BASE/QUOTE is the right to buy (call) or sell (put) the base currency against the quote currency at the strike K, exercised at the expiry time on the expiry date and settled on the settlement date, which for a tenor is the forward’s value date; the expiry is the latest date whose spot date is that settlement date (the inverse of the spot rule; where no date has it, around a US Labor Day, the spot lag is counted back and the ticket says so), by delivery of both currencies or, for a non-deliverable option, in the quote currency against a fixing. It is valued with Garman and Kohlhagen (1983), which is Black–Scholes with the base currency as the dividend-paying asset, on the same forward the currency forward uses (§12: covered interest parity from the spot date, or the account’s quoted points), discounted in the quote currency to the settlement date:
C=Nb​Pq​(Ts​)[FΦ(d1​)−KΦ(d2​)],P=Nb​Pq​(Ts​)[KΦ(−d2​)−FΦ(−d1​)],d1,2​=σTe​​ln(F/K)±21​σ2Te​​,​(36)

with Te​ the ACT/365 time to expiry and Ts​ to settlement, F the forward to settlement and Nb​ the base notional. A sold option carries the opposite sign. The premium is a cash flow on its payment date, not part of the value once paid; a non-deliverable option has the same value as a deliverable one.

Volatility. A pair’s surface is saved as the market quotes it, per tenor: the at-the-money vol, the 25-delta risk reversal RR=σ25Δc​−σ25Δp​ and the 25-delta butterfly BF=21​(σ25Δc​+σ25Δp​)−σATM​. Across strikes the smile is Malz’s quadratic in the call’s forward delta,
σ(Δ)=σATM​−2RR(Δ−21​)+16BF(Δ−21​)2,(37)

which reproduces the three quotes exactly and is solved as a fixed point with Δ=Φ(d1​) (the premium-excluded forward delta). ATM, RR and BF are interpolated linearly in time between quoted tenors and held flat beyond them; a tenor quoted ATM-only contributes to the level and not to the skew. Conventions stated as limitations: the ATM quote is applied at Δ=21​ (in this delta convention d1​=0, the delta-neutral straddle premium excluded), so the vol read at K=F sits off it: a hundredth of a point at G10 levels, but 0.1 to 0.5 points at one month and up to 0.8 at one year on a 40% surface with a put skew (the sign follows the skew), and more at higher vols; the smile is a quadratic through three points, so outside the 25-delta strikes it is an extrapolation whose error grows towards the wings (§13, digital assets, gives measured sizes); premium-included deltas (the standard for USD-base pairs) are not used. Without a saved surface the pair prices at a flat desk default and the response says so; the daily demo build writes a synthetic surface for the G10 pairs, labelled as such, since no public source quotes FX vols.

Risk. In the desk’s taxonomy: spot01 (+1% spot, repriced; the forward moves with spot, the discounting does not), the equivalent spot position in base units, gamma over a further 1%, vega per volatility point (repriced), IR01 on each curve (+1bp, repriced: the quote curve raises the forward and lowers the discount factor, the base curve lowers the forward), theta one calendar day later. The ticket shows the forward delta beside them.

In the frameworks. The P&L explain gains a vol step after spot and points: the pair’s surface is moved tenor bucket by tenor bucket, so a day’s vega P&L is a row of its own and only cross terms reach the residual (§11). The risk ladder bumps each surface bucket by one volatility point and reports vega by (surface, bucket), kept apart from the rate ladder (docs/market_risk.md); Volatility is a VaR factor: each surface’s quotes (ATM, risk reversal and butterfly per tenor; a swaption’s ATM grid point by point) are moved by their observed daily changes beside the curves and spots and every option is repriced in full; a surface is secondary to the curves and spots, held still on a day it has no observation, and the page says how many of the window’s days each surface covered. The hosted demo’s surfaces have no public source, so their level is scaled day by day by the realised vol of the series they sit on, labelled as such (risk/vols.py).

On the exposure paths the option is valued before expiry with Garman–Kohlhagen on the path’s forward (the path’s spot and bonds) at the surface’s forward vol for its remaining life and the smile at its moneyness, and after expiry as the payoff fixed on the spot at the expiry grid point and discounted until settlement (§9, §15).

The canonical record (§17) carries the fields of the ISDA FX and Currency Option Definitions: pair, option type, exercise style, both notionals, strike, expiry date and time, settlement date and type, settlement currency and fixing source for a non-deliverable option, premium amount, currency and payment date, automatic exercise; buyer and seller are named by LEI so both bookings hash identically.
Styles. (pricing/fx_exotic.py.) The same dynamics price the other styles a currency desk trades, each with its QuantLib benchmark:

items.html: American: a Leisen–Reimer binomial tree (801 steps) with early exercise at every node; within 0.02bp of notional of QuantLib’s QD+ fixed-point engine and to rounding of its own Leisen–Reimer tree. Where the strike is about 170 standard deviations or more from the forward the tree’s probabilities reach 0 or 1 and it has no step sizes; the value there is the best of exercising along the drift Sebt: now, at expiry (the European value), or at the interior time where Sebt=Kr/rb​ when there is one (within 0.2bp of notional of QuantLib on both sides of that point; before 9 November 2026 these terms raised an error). No ticket at a market vol reaches it.
Digital: a fixed quote-currency amount (cash-or-nothing) or a fixed base amount (asset-or-nothing scaled), Reiner–Rubinstein closed forms; to rounding against AnalyticEuropeanEngine.

Barrier (up or down, in or out, with a rebate paid at the hit for a knock-out and at expiry for a knock-in): the knock-out value is the integral of the payoff against the survival density of log-spot with one absorbing barrier, built by the method of images with the drift restored by Girsanov, and knock-in = vanilla − knock-out; within 2×10−3bp of notional of AnalyticBarrierEngine across all eight cases.
Double barrier: the same integral with the two-barrier image series (Ikeda–Kunitomo); within 2×10−3bp of AnalyticDoubleBarrierEngine.

Touch: one-touch and no-touch from the first-passage and survival probabilities (paid at the hit or at expiry), double no-touch from the two-barrier density, double one-touch as its complement; against AnalyticDigitalAmericanEngine, its knock-out variant and AnalyticDoubleBarrierBinaryEngine. The value of one unit paid at the first hit, (H/S)μ+λΦ(ηz)+(H/S)μ−λΦ(ηz−2ηλσT​), is evaluated term by term in logarithms: written as a power times Φ it lost its first term wherever Φ underflowed while the power was large (∣b∣T​/σ above about 3.7: up to 4.7% of the payout at a vol of one or two percent, exact at the vols of the pairs quoted here; found and corrected on 9 November 2026 against a quadrature of the hitting density, which is also what is used when the discount rate is so far below zero that λ is not real). The same term is the knock-out’s rebate.

blocks.html: Barriers are monitored continuously; the vol is the smile vol at the strike, held flat across the barrier (vanna–volga is the next step; QuantLib’s analytic barrier engines are flat-vol as well).

On a ticket’s exposure paths a barrier is watched on the grid dates and between them: where the level stood inside at both ends a and b of a step that accumulated variance v, it crossed B on the way with probability exp(−2ln(a/B)ln(b/B)/v) (the Brownian bridge’s crossing probability; with volatility regimes v is the step’s own on each path), and one uniform per path and step decides it. Against the continuous closed forms on a six-month knock-out at 55% volatility, 40,000 paths: the share of paths that touch is within 0.2% on weekly and on monthly steps, and the knock-out’s payoff on the paths is within about 1% of its price. Watched on the dates alone (until 0.30.0) weekly steps missed 16% of the touches and paid 63% more than the price, monthly steps 29% and 126%. A corridor adds its two sides’ probabilities, capped at one; every option leg of a package reads the same touches, so a knock-in and a knock-out of the same terms remain the plain option. The credit page’s netting-set engine still watches on its dates alone. An American option is valued as its European (the early-exercise premium is not simulated), as docs/ccr.md says. The vol along the paths is the surface’s, not one number held: the spot steps with the piecewise forward vols of the ATM term structure, so its log-variance at every grid date is the surface’s ATM variance there, and at each date the option is valued at the forward vol for its remaining life with the quoted risk reversal and butterfly at the remaining tenor read at the delta of the path’s own forward against the strike (sticky-delta, the FX convention); a touch, which has no strike, takes the forward ATM vol. The same functions (pricing/fx_vol.py: step_vols, path_vols) serve the ticket’s stand-alone XVA and the credit engine.
Vol of vol is not modelled: the surface’s level does not move along a path, which a stochastic-vol model would add and is on the roadmap with its own validation gate.

The canonical record carries the style, the payout and its currency, the barrier type and levels, the rebate, the touch type, whether a touch pays at the hit, and the monitoring convention. The ticket’s scenario tab reprices every style on a grid of spot and vol shocks through the engine itself. The trade’s structure in the blotter is its style, so a digital, a barrier and a touch are told apart at a glance and found by search.

Digital assets. An option on BTC, ETH or SOL against USD is the same product with the asset’s funding rate rc​ as the base rate: the forward is the cash-and-carry one of §12, b=rUSD​−rc​, discounting in USD to settlement the day after expiry, settlement in cash against the settlement price source (a non-deliverable option in the ISDA Digital Asset Derivatives Definitions’ vocabulary; the canonical record is the CRYPTO_OPTION product, which keeps its pre-November byte shape for a European and carries the style’s terms otherwise). Every style of §13 prices on the same engine; the reference table carries rows at crypto parameters (spot 65 000, funding 3%, vol 60%).

The desk’s taxonomy names the sensitivities: FX01 is the spot delta of a currency pair and CRY01 that of a digital asset (PV for +1% spot); on a digital asset IR01 is the discounting curve’s sensitivity alone and the forward basis’s is CRYBASIS01: the change in value for +1bp a year on the basis ln(F/S)/T at fixed spot and USD curve, a long forward positive, computed as the negative of the +1bp bump of the asset’s rate (FUND01, which the API still reports), which agrees with the exact basis bump to about 10−4T of itself (T in years: 2.5×10−5 on a three-month forward, 10−3 at ten years; on an option the difference is convexity in the forward, 8×10−5 on a three-month at-the-money call); it is one flat bucket, not a tenor ladder. On a currency pair both legs are rate curves and the ticket shows the two currencies’ IR01 apart.

The surfaces {ASSET}USD_VOL have the FX shape and, from 9 November 2026, come from a venue: Deribit’s public option chain gives each instrument’s mark volatility and the forward of its expiry (market_data/deribit.py; BTC and ETH from their own chains, SOL from the USDC-settled one). Per expiry every strike’s mark is placed at its premium-excluded forward call delta Φ(d1​), the convention of the smile above, and the vol is read linearly in delta at 41​, 21​ and 43​: ATM=σ(21​), RR=σ(41​)−σ(43​), BF=21​(σ(41​)+σ(43​))−σ(21​), so at a tenor the quadratic returns the venue’s marks at those three points; ATM is the 50-delta-forward vol, not the vol at the forward strike.

Across expiries ATM is interpolated linearly in total variance and RR, BF linearly in time to ten tenors (the FX grid with two and three weeks added, where the listed term structure is steepest); beyond the last listed expiry all three are held flat, and the row’s source names that expiry. Between tenors the pricer interpolates linearly in vol as for any pair, so a listed expiry that does not fall on a tenor is not reproduced exactly: within 0.3 of a vol point on the term structure of 9 November 2026, and up to 1.3 points on steeper or event-shaped ones (measured on constructed term structures); inside one week it holds the one-week level, which a steep front end misses by 2.5 to 10 points at four days on the shapes tested. The builder dates an expiry to the hour (08:00 UTC) while the pricer counts whole days, which alone moves a three- to four-day premium by 2 to 3%.

The forward of each expiry over the venue’s index gives an annualised basis ln(F/S)/T, interpolated linearly in time and held flat beyond the last expiry out to the two-year tenor, stored as forward points {ASSET}USD_FWD (the feed’s grid ends at two years; beyond it the pricer carries the last basis on as a rate, as for any pair, and a tenor beyond the venue’s last listed expiry is reported as implied); on the account’s market forward mode the forward is spot plus those points and the funding rate is the one they imply, while a funding rate named on a forward ticket takes precedence for that price and the forward is then the cash-and-carry one at that rate (the option ticket has no funding field and always sits on the account’s forward). CRYBASIS01 keeps its meaning under quoted points: +1bp of basis raises each outright by FT⋅1bp, and the ladder moves the points by that.

The response is read under a size cap and a deadline and only finite numbers are used; the marks must be dated within thirty minutes and the venue’s index within 5% of the spot fetched in the same run. Within an expiry a mark more than a quarter away from the median of the five marks around it (the worst first, re-read after each removal), or whose delta breaks the order of the strikes, is left out; three stale marks side by side are not seen by this and are left to the bounds; an expiry is left out when it is inside two days, has fewer than six usable marks, has no open interest, does not reach the 25-delta points, gives a level outside sanity bounds or a forward too far from the index; a surface needs two usable expiries. The marks are refreshed several times an hour; when the venue does not answer the last surface stands and its own time stays in the source printed on the ticket.

Known limitations: the marks are one venue’s, a mark is the venue’s model fit rather than a trade, tenors beyond the last listed expiry (about ten months for BTC and ETH, less for SOL) are an extrapolation; the chain’s other strikes are not stored, so the smile away from the three points is the quadratic’s and no residual of that fit is kept: on test smiles that are not quadratic (an SVI, a parabola in log-moneyness) the 10-delta strike on the skew side priced 2 to 3 vol points, 12 to 19% of premium, below the smile it was built from, and the 5-delta strike 5 to 9 points below (a third to a half of its premium); reading linearly in delta between marks biases ATM up by about a tenth of a point on a sparse strike grid; CRYBASIS01 under quoted points is exact to the last quoted tenor and, beyond it, to first order (the bump of the last tenor carries through the held basis; until v1.13 the points were held there and it read a third low at three years); the forward points are not yet a factor of the VaR of §14, and the exposure paths of §15 still drift a digital asset at the stored flat funding rate rather than at the venue’s basis.

Fixings and settlement. A digital-asset forward or option settles in cash against the settlement price source its record names, on its valuation date (a forward) or expiration date (an option). A forward’s valuation date is its fixing date, a field of the ticket: after the trade date and on or before the settlement date; the settlement date itself for the venue’s morning price, one day earlier for a benchmark, unless changed. Before the fixing date a forward that fixes at Tf​ and is paid at Tp​≥Tf​ is the forward of the fixing date, discounted from the payment date: V=±N(F(Tf​)−K)Dq​(Tp​), an amount known at Tf​ and paid at Tp​. (Until 0.26.0 the forward was carried to Tp​, overstating the carry by Sbg/365 for a gap of g days, and the gap was limited to seven days; there is no limit now.) The exposure simulation of such a forward starts from this value and runs the level on to the payment date, where the amount is in fact fixed from Tf​: over a gap of days this is small, and it is not a model of a forward that fixes months before it is paid. The counterparty exposure report and the capital built on it, and a forward leg of a package, still carry the forward to Tp​. Whether a barrier or a touch level traded on the way is not something a fixing can say: the desk records it (the day the level traded, or, once the option has expired, that it never did), and the record is not a term of the signed confirmation. With a touch recorded the option settles on a final amount; before expiry it is valued for what it has become: a knock-in as the plain option, a knock-out and a no-touch as nothing outstanding, a one-touch as its payout (nothing, where it was paid at the hit). Without a record the amount at expiry stays provisional, valued as never touched, with the other amount beside it.

Fixings are stored per pair, date and source: the venue’s daily delivery price (its index averaged over the thirty minutes before 08:00 UTC), read once a day and never overwritten by the feed, and a desk’s own entry for a benchmark. The venue’s price is stored only for a date it can have published and only within 15% of the template account’s stored spot of that date (else of the day before, else the day after); this catches gross errors, not a wrong fixing inside the band, and a genuine fixing after a larger move is refused until an administrator stores it with a reason. A later read of the venue that differs from a stored fixing stores nothing and marks the date disputed. The fixing of a trade is the stored value for exactly its named source; another source’s price is never substituted.

A booked valuation names its state. live: before the fixing date, the pricer above. fixed: from the fixing date the amount ±N(X−K), X the fixing, or an option’s payoff at X, is one cash flow on the settlement date, discounted on the quote currency’s OIS curve; its only sensitivities are IR01 =PV(e−1bpt−1) and one day’s theta; spot, funding and vega are zero, and an out-of-the-money option reports zero throughout. settled: from the settlement date the value is zero and the amount is reported. The amount is provisional, and says why, in two cases. With no fixing stored for the named source the stored spot of the fixing date stands in for it, valued as the same single cash flow. A barrier or touch is final only when the fixing is itself at or beyond the barrier or the trade records its knock state; otherwise the amount is the one that holds if the barrier was never touched, the amount if it was is reported beside it, and neither is a bound on the other. A touch that pays at the hit, and a knock-out’s rebate, recorded as touched have been paid at the hit and nothing is outstanding at expiry.

Known limitations: the settlement amount is reported and not yet booked as a cash event, and on the fixing day the P&L explain shows the move to the fixing as carry rather than as a spot step; the state is by date, so a trade reads fixed from the start of its fixing day, provisional until the fixing is stored; nothing in the application records a knock state or the date of a hit, and a recorded state is not used before expiry; the venue’s delivery price and a 4pm London benchmark are different numbers, so a trade’s economics depend on the source chosen at booking; the ticket’s scenario tab reprices in the browser, for forwards and European options only, with the closed form above (its normal distribution to 10−7, so to cents with no shock) and the same interpolation of forward points, scaling the quoted points with a spot shock (12.5bp of spot at ±10%, three months, a 5% basis): the interpolation, the settlement amounts and a forward’s repricing are pinned to the engine’s by shared test vectors.

A forward’s scenario starts from the engine’s own forward F and spot lag ts​, both in the pricer’s answer, and moves them as the engine would: F′=F(1+s)e(Δq​−Δb​)(T−ts​) and Pq′​(T)=Pq​(T)e−Δq​T for a spot shock s and parallel shifts Δq​, Δb​ of the two rates, the forward carried from the spot date and the discount factor from today; a tenor dragged on the chart adds its change in forward points at the settlement date, moved by the same two factors, and F′ is held at no less than 1% of spot. On a forward implied from the two curves this is the engine priced again, to rounding: with no shock, under a spot shock and under a rate shock (six forwards on flat curves, four of them with a spot lag, in the shared vectors; no non-deliverable forward and no trade settling at spot is among them, and a dragged tenor is not compared with the engine). On quoted points it is the engine’s value with no shock only: the tab scales the points with a spot shock where the engine adds the same points to the moved spot (the points times the shock: 2.5 pips on a three-month EURUSD at +5%), and the engine holds a quoted forward when a curve moves, so there the two rate sliders show the carry effect alone, which the tab states; no vector covers quoted points. (Before 9 November 2026 the tab rebuilt a parity forward from the two discount factors counted from today, and the unshocked scenario of a currency pair was off by the carry over the spot lag: 1.6 pips on a three-month EURUSD at 3.9% against 2.1%; and it moved the forward under a rate shock over today to settlement, 0.8bp of the forward too far at 100bp and three days.) An option’s forward moves by the same rule; its repricing as a whole is not compared with the engine. Its volatility is shocked flat, in vol points, or tenor by tenor of the pair’s stored surface: the option is repriced at the volatility it priced at moved by the shock at its own expiry, read on the straight line in time between the two tenors around it (the end tenor’s beyond them), so the smile moves in level and not in shape. A package’s option legs read the same tenor shocks each at its own expiry.

Who prices a scenario. A single trade is priced under a scenario by the engine, at the market the tab works out by the rules above. A spot, a forward or a non-deliverable forward is valued by the pricer’s own line, ±N(F′−K)Pq′​, with Pq′​ the discount factor to the date the amount is paid; a European option by the function the ticket was priced with, on F′ and Pq′​(T) themselves and the time to expiry the ticket reports, not through rates read back out of them. With no shock both are the ticket’s own figures: a forward’s to the last digit, an option’s to the last digits of its volatility, which travels as volatility points. The browser has the same closed form for these two and shows it for a figure while the engine’s answer is on its way, or when none comes (the tab then says so), so that a figure follows a drag; it agrees with the engine to a thousandth of a cent on ten million (until version 1.29 its normal distribution function was a five-term polynomial, good to seven places, and a European option stood up to one unit of the quote currency from the engine on that size). The market itself is the tab’s, with the limits stated above: on quoted points a spot shock scales the points and a curve shock moves the forward by its carry, where the pricer would add the same points to the moved spot and hold the quoted forward. A forward paid after its fixing is discounted under a shock by the curve of the currency it is paid in: P′=Pe−Δq​Tp​ when paid in the quote currency at Tp​, and P′=Pe−Δq​T−Δb​(Tp​−T) when paid in the base currency, the base curve carrying the amount over the days from the fixing to the payment, as in pricing. A package of legs is not sent to the engine: its figures are the closed form over its legs, and the tab labels them an approximation.

An option of another style under a scenario. The browser has no closed form for an American, digital, barrier, double-barrier or touch option: it is priced under a scenario by the engine alone, and a figure with no answer yet is a dash. The tab works out what the scenario does to the four inputs the pricer takes, by the rules above: the spot S′=S(1+s), the forward to settlement F′, the quote discount factor Pq′​(T) and the volatility σ′=σ+Δσ, with σ the volatility the ticket priced at, unrounded. The engine values the style there with the function the ticket was priced with, reading the inputs as it does in pricing, rq​=−lnPq′​(T)/Te​ and b=ln(F′/S′)/Te​ over the time to expiry Te​, and returns the value alone (one valuation a state, where pricing makes eleven for its risk figures). With no shock the four inputs are the ticket’s and the figure is the ticket’s own, to the last digit. A spot shock of +1% with nothing else moved is the one-sided revaluation that defines the ticket’s value of a 1% rise in spot (its FX01 or CRY01; not the two-sided delta in units of the base currency), the forward moving with spot and the carry held, and a shock of one volatility point is the one that defines its vega, so those two columns are the ticket’s own figures. A rate shock is not the pricer’s own bump. A shift Δq​ of the quote curve moves the discount factor by e−Δq​T to the settlement date T and the forward by eΔq​(T−ts​), which the pricer reads over the time to expiry: rq​ moves by Δq​T/Te​ and b by Δq​(T−ts​)/Te​, so the base rate rq​−b moves by Δq​ts​/Te​; the pricer’s bump for IR01 moves rq​ and b by Δq​ exactly and holds the base rate. A shift Δb​ of the base rate moves b by −Δb​(T−ts​)/Te​ where the pricer’s bump moves it by −Δb​. The scenario’s rate columns therefore differ from IR01 times the shock by the settlement and spot lags over the time to expiry: about 7% for a one-month option that settles two days after it expires, under 1% beyond a year. Every limit of the forward’s scenario above holds here too: on quoted points the tab scales the points with spot and moves the forward with the two rates, where the engine would not. The volatility is one number held at the strike while spot and the forward move (the surface is not read again), and a barrier or touch option is priced on that one volatility as in pricing.

A shock may carry the spot to a barrier or beyond it, where the pricer, which takes a spot inside the barriers, has no value. The option is then valued as touched at that spot, at the limit of the pricer’s value as the spot comes to the barrier, with what the touch pays counted in, so the scenario’s value does not jump when a shock crosses: a knock-out is worth its rebate, paid then (nothing for a double barrier, which carries none); a knock-in is the plain option at that spot, its own rebate lost; a one-touch is its payout, in full when paid at the hit and discounted from settlement when paid at expiry; a no-touch is worth nothing; a double one-touch is its payout discounted from settlement, as the pricer values it. The terms are checked against the spot the ticket was priced at, which also says on which side a single touch level stands. The tab marks a scenario, and each column of its ladder, in which the level is touched. Tests hold that the ticket’s own state gives the ticket’s value exactly for each of fourteen options (every style, both barrier directions, in and out, with and without a rebate), that a shocked state inside the barriers is the pricer at those inputs, that the limit of the pricer’s value at each barrier (the line through its values two millionths and one millionth of spot inside, read at the barrier) is the touched value to a thousandth of the quote currency on ten million of notional or a payout of 250,000, the value a millionth inside being itself within 15, and what each touched style is worth; in the browser, that +1% of spot and one volatility point move each style by the ticket’s own spot delta and vega to 10% (a tolerance for a ticket that prices itself again during the check, not for a difference in method), and that a point on every tenor of the surface is the flat point. There is no outside reference of its own: the value at a state is the pricer whose prices are compared with QuantLib (§18), and the touched values are the standard limits of those payoffs. Not covered: a package holding such an option is not repriced whole (the tab then shows its first leg alone and says so); the spot delta beside a shock that crosses a barrier is a first-order figure and means little there, which the ladder shows.

Beside the scenario’s fixing the tab states what the option would settle by its terms, the reading the settlement rule makes for a digital asset (Fixings and settlement, above): a plain option and a digital by the fixing alone; a barrier or a touch by whether its level traded on the way, which a fixing short of the level cannot say, so both amounts are given, and one alone when the fixing itself stands at or beyond the level.

For an option the tab also draws the pair’s surface as the pricer reads it (ATM, risk reversal and butterfly linear in time between the quoted tenors and flat beyond them, the smile in forward call delta, the vol at the strike by the same fixed point), pinned to the engine’s reading by the same vectors; a vol shock is drawn as the surface moved in parallel, with the strike left at its unshocked delta. The Methodology tab’s workbooks rebuild the European option and the styles at crypto parameters beside the engine’s values.

Reference. Against QuantLib’s GarmanKohlagenProcess with AnalyticEuropeanEngine on the same spot, rates and vol: value to rounding for calls and puts, bought and sold, in and out of the money, to two years; delta in base units to rounding; the repriced spot01, vega and rate sensitivities within the second- and third-order terms of their bumps (§18). The smile reproduces its three quotes at their own strikes. The styles above are in the same table.

Replication. The Methodology tab’s workbooks rebuild the European option (Garman–Kohlhagen with its delta and vega), the digitals, the eight single-barrier cases with rebates (Reiner–Rubinstein’s terms A–F), the touches, and the double barriers and double touches (the two-barrier image series summed one row per image) with live Excel formulas beside the engine’s values: the closed forms are the independent check of the engine’s numerical integration, and agree with it to better than 10−6 of value. The American option is a tree and has no spreadsheet form; its check is QuantLib’s.

sections.title: Market risk: ladder, VaR, stress, backtesting

blocks.html: The ladder

For every live trade and every curve it is valued on, each tenor bucket’s quotes are bumped +1bp and the trade repriced on the as-of market through the production pricers; the result is key-rate IR01 by (curve, bucket), the buckets (0–1Y, 1–5Y, 5–10Y, 10Y+) the same the P&L explain uses. Spot deltas are the pricers’ PV for +1% spot: FX01 on a currency pair, CRY01 on a digital asset. On a digital asset IR01 is the discounting curve’s sensitivity alone and the forward basis’s is CRYBASIS01 (the negative of the asset-rate bump FUND01), reported beside the IR01 totals and never summed into them. A volatility surface the trade is valued on ({PAIR}_VOL, {CCY}_SWVOL_ATM) is bumped +1 vol point per tenor bucket, a swaption grid by expiry, and reported as vega by (surface, bucket). A par bump of every quote is a slightly smaller move in zero rates, so the ladder total sits about 2% below the ticket’s IR01, which bumps zero rates; the bucket values agree with a QuantLib rebootstrap to 0.05% of DV01 (§18).

At each quoted tenor. A bucket moves its quotes together, so a two-year position against a five-year one nets inside the 1–5Y bucket and the ladder by bucket cannot tell it from no position. Beside each bucket the ladder therefore carries the points it is made of: every quoted tenor of the curve is bumped +1bp on its own, the curve rebuilt and the trade repriced, giving KR01 by (curve, quoted tenor); a surface is bumped +1 vol point at one tenor (all of that tenor’s rows, as a bucket moves them) and a swaption grid +1bp of normal vol at one expiry, giving vega by (surface, tenor). This is the risk at the instrument one would hedge with. A bucket that carries under a hundredth of a trade’s largest bucket on the curve is not broken into its points (a five-year swap is priced a little off each of the sixteen quotes of its first year and not at all off the thirty-year one): its own figure stands. Such a bucket is first moved once more, unevenly, its first quote by one basis point, its second by two and so on, and is broken into its points after all if that moves the trade, so that a small net figure made of large points that cancel is not passed over. The points cost a pricing each: on the twelve-trade test book the report takes about twice as long (2.9s to 6.1s). A bucket’s figure is still measured by moving the bucket whole by a basis point, so nothing that reads the buckets (the VaR’s linear comparison, the limits, the P&L explain) changes. A point is measured as a slope: the quote is moved by a hundredth of a basis point and the change scaled to one. The reason is that one par quote moved alone by a whole basis point swings the forward rates on either side of it by several basis points in opposite directions, and an option is not linear over that: with each point moved a whole basis point, a cap’s points came to 13.5% more than its bucket, and to 0.13% more at a hundredth. So a trade’s points add up to its bucket to within the bucket’s own convexity over a basis point: 0.03% for a five-year swap, about 1% for a cap, a floor or a collar on the test book. The rate risk of a cap carries the move of its volatility with the forward, because the cap surface is held by distance from the money (§6); the ticket’s IR01 holds the volatility where it was. The response of the curve to one quote is checked against QuantLib: a single quote moved by a basis point, the curve rebuilt and a swap repriced agree to 0.034% of the trade’s DV01 (§18), which checks the points where the risk is; a point far smaller than that, at a quote away from the trade’s own tenors, takes its sign and size from the curve’s interpolation (three builds of the same curve give +0.4, −1.2 and −4.5 at the nine-year quote of a ten-year swap whose DV01 is 8,520) and is not a position. The independent price verification (§11) moves each row of a surface on its own; the ladder moves a tenor’s rows together, as its buckets do. A funding level has one quote and no points; a point that moves a trade by less than a millionth of its currency is not carried. The trader’s home draws a column for a tenor that carries at least 3% of its factor’s largest point; the Market risk page lists every one.
Historical simulation by full revaluation

The risk factors are the curve quotes (par rates in basis points, tenor by tenor), the spots (log returns) and the volatility surfaces (every quote of an FX surface: ATM, 25-delta risk reversal and butterfly per tenor; the swaption ATM grid point by point). For each day i of the window today’s market M is shifted by that day’s observed changes Δi​ and every trade repriced:
P&Li​=trades∑​[NPV(M+Δi​)−NPV(M)]⋅fx,VaRq​=−Qq​{P&Li​},ESq​=−E[P&Li​∣P&Li​<−VaRq​],​(38)

the horizon scaled by h​. The curves and spots define the window: only days on which every one of them has an observation are used, and a factor with no history is listed on the page, not dropped. A volatility surface is a secondary factor: on a day it was observed its quotes move with the rest, on a day it was not it is held still, and the page states each surface’s coverage of the window. The bootstrapped curves are cached per shifted market; beyond a budget of valuations the full revaluation is skipped and the ladder VaR reported, with a note. The ladder VaR is computed alongside as the linear comparison,
P&Liladder​=c,b∑​KR01[c,b]Δi​[c,b]+a∑​spot01[a]ri​[a]+s,b∑​vega[s,b]Δσi​[s,b],(39)

and the difference between the two is the convexity and the inside-bucket curve shape the ladder cannot see. Defaults: confidence 99% (95% secondary), one day, a 730-day window, sixty observations minimum.
History and the demo’s surfaces

The demo’s rates market is synthetic (since version 1.38). No interest-rate number of the hosted demo comes from a publisher: not an overnight fixing, not a government yield, not a swap quote. The recipe, in full. Each curve is a Nelson–Siegel par curve, y(t)=β0​+β1​f1​(t/τ)+β2​f2​(t/τ) with f1​(x)=(1−e−x)/x and f2​(x)=f1​(x)−e−x, in per cent, t in years: β0​ is the long end, β0​+β1​ the overnight rate, β2​ the hump. The four parameters (β0​,β1​,β2​,τ) of each currency were set by hand on 17 November 2026 to look like a market of that time (USD 4.30,−0.45,−1.00,2.0; EUR 2.90,−0.95,−0.60,2.5; GBP 4.45,−0.50,−0.90,2.0; CHF 0.80,−0.75,−0.30,3.0; JPY 2.40,−1.90,−0.50,4.0): on that day a curve is its parameters, and they follow nothing after it. On every other business day (Monday to Friday; no holiday calendar) three factors have moved the curve, level (added to β0​), slope (β1​) and curvature (β2​). A factor is zero on the set day and walks from it one business day at a time, forwards and backwards: Fnext day out​=ϕFday nearer​+σsεday out​, in per cent, with ϕ=e−0.05/252 (a mean reversion of 5% a year, the policy of the exposure engine, §15), a daily σ of 3.5, 2.0 and 1.5 bp for the three factors, and a scale s per currency (USD 1.00, EUR 0.85, GBP 1.05, CHF 0.60, JPY 0.50), also set by hand. The shock is ε(curve,factor,day)=0.5​n(all,factor,day)+0.5​n(curve,factor,day), so every currency shares half of each shock’s variance; n(⋅) is a standard normal made from the SHA-256 hash of the text rijeka synthetic rates 1|key|key|..., where the factor’s key is one of the words level, slope, curvature, the curve’s key is its id (USD\_SOFR, EUR\_ESTR, GBP\_SONIA, CHF\_SARON, JPY\_TONAR) and the day is written as its proleptic Gregorian ordinal, so the level shock all currencies shared on 18 November 2026 is hashed from rijeka synthetic rates 1|all|level|739938 and the dollar curve’s own from rijeka synthetic rates 1|USD\_SOFR|level|739938: u1​=(first 8 bytes, big-endian+1)/(264+1), u2​=(next 8 bytes)/264, n=−2lnu1​​cos(2πu2​). A weekend carries Friday’s curve. The pillars are the 33 tenors of the curves page, the overnight point read at 1/365 of a year; a stored quote is the function’s value rounded to four decimals (the function itself does not round, and reads a maturity below 10−6 of a year as 10−6). A curve is therefore a pure function of the currency and the date: today’s quotes, any day’s overnight fixing and a history of any length are the same function and cannot disagree (market\_data/synthetic\_rates.py; the recipe, with the seed, is also on the public endpoint GET /api/market-data/demo/sources; a test rebuilds a shock from this text alone and a factor’s first two steps by hand). The curve ids keep the names of the conventions each is bootstrapped with (day count, calendar, settlement lag); the default quotes shown on the curves page before the API answers are the set day’s curves, written by a script from the same recipe (backend/scripts/synthetic\_rates\_defaults.py; a test fails if the file is not what the script makes). What it does, measured. Over the four years to the set day a ten-year rate moved 3.6 bp a day in USD, 3.1 in EUR, 3.7 in GBP, 2.1 in CHF and 1.8 in JPY, with a correlation of 0.50 between the daily changes of USD and EUR; the three-month rate’s annual volatility, which the real-world exposure calibration reads, was 65, 56, 66, 38 and 32 bp. A level wanders from the set day like a slow random walk: about σsn​ after n business days (80 bp in two years at scale one), at most σs/1−ϕ2​=176 bp times the scale in the long run. Over twenty years, ten each side of the set day, the quotes ran from 1.5 to 5.9% in USD and from −1.6 to 1.2% in CHF, and all 2,610 curves sampled (five currencies, fortnightly) bootstrapped, with one-month forwards between −1.6 and 5.9%. The model validator rebuilt a ten-year rate from an implementation of the formula of the validator’s own, on the engine’s shocks, to fifteen digits (18 November 2026, on the first version of the factors; the mean reversion was then far too fast, about 3.8 a year, and was changed to the present one on the validator’s finding). On the present version the validator wrote an implementation from this paragraph alone, before reading the code, and reproduced six rates bit for bit (the dollar ten-year on three dates either side of the set day, the euro overnight, the yen ten-year two years back, the franc five-year in June 2027), having had to guess the hash’s key words, which are printed above since. What follows from it. A price, a sensitivity or an adjustment of the demo is exact arithmetic on a market that is not one. The rates history that VaR, the backtest and the real-world calibration of counterparty exposure read is this generator’s: Gaussian daily moves with no jumps and no meeting dates, around hand-set levels of one day. Those figures describe the generator and not any market’s tail. The Swiss franc curve sits near zero and its short end is below zero about as often as above. The exposure engine’s real-world mean reversion is 0.05 a year by policy, which is the generator’s; the two-year AR(1) estimate shown beside it is at its upper bound of 0.50 on every window measured, as it is on any near-random walk of that length, which is why the policy and not the estimate is used. The Federal Reserve’s published projections on the home page are the Fed’s; the implied path drawn beside them is read from the synthetic curve and says so. Reports stored before the switch (a day’s P&L, a VaR, a backtest pair) were struck on the earlier market and are not comparable with those after it; the stored rates history is replaced as a whole when it is rebuilt, so no window mixes the two. Until version 1.38 the curves were built daily from published overnight fixings and government par yields with a stated spread schedule; the firm holds no licence for any benchmark, and the administrators of some require one to build a curve from or to value with. Spots are still read from public sources: ECB reference rates for currency pairs, a venue’s daily closes for digital assets; each day’s values are stored as the template account’s snapshot, so the daily rebuild extends the series.

No public source quotes implied volatility for rates or currency pairs, so those surfaces are synthetic in shape and market-driven in level: each day the parametric surface’s ATM is scaled by σtenor windowreal​/σseriesreal​​ from the stored spot series (an FX pair, a digital asset) or from the 5Y par rate’s changes (the swaption grid), clipped to [21​,2], risk reversals and butterflies as quoted; every such row is labelled. (The one-week row is the exception: its window of five changes is below the estimator’s minimum of ten, so its scale is always one and the row does not move day to day.) A desk with a feed stores its own surfaces under the same ids.

The digital-asset surfaces are a venue’s marks from 9 November 2026 (§13) and a built row never replaces one; the dates before the venue’s first surface are rebuilt from it, ATM(t,d)=ATMvenue(t)⋅s(t,d)/s(t,d0​) with s the scale above and d0​ the first venue date, its risk reversals and butterflies held, so the series has no step on the day the source changed (the ratio of two clipped scales lies in [41​,4], and the level of the whole back-history depends on the scale on d0​). That rebuild takes effect when the history is next backfilled; until then a window containing d0​ samples the change of source as one day’s move in vol, and the VaR of a book with digital-asset options is to be read with that in mind.
Stress

Named scenarios by full revaluation: every trade repriced on the shifted market. Rates scenarios shift quotes in basis points, parallel or by bucket (parallel ±25, ±100bp; steepener and flattener ±25 short against long); FX scenarios move the non-USD asset by a percentage, a USD-first quote the other way (USD ±10%); digital assets ±30%; a combined risk-off (rates −50bp, USD +5%, digital assets −30%); and the vol scenarios move the FX surfaces’ ATM rows by a number of points (larger for the digital assets) and the swaption grid by bp of normal vol. A rate scenario leaves the surfaces alone. A trade whose pricer cannot value the shifted market is listed under the scenario, not summed as zero.
Limits and backtesting

A limit names a metric (VAR_99_1D, ES_99_1D, IR01, IR01:<curve>, KR01:<curve>:<bucket>, SPOT01:<asset>, NPV, STRESS:<scenario>), a scope and a value; utilisation is ∣value∣/limit with a warning level and a breach at 100%, evaluated on every member’s book after the daily run. Backtesting pairs every stored P&L date with the VaR standing the evening before; an exception is a day whose loss exceeded it, on the clean (positions held at the previous close), hypothetical (clean without carry) or dirty P&L. The count is read two ways: the Basel traffic light from the cumulative binomial at the stated confidence (green below 95%, yellow to 99.99%, red beyond: at 250 days and 99%, 0–4 / 5–9 / 10+), and Kupiec’s proportion-of-failures test, LR=−2ln[(1−p)n−xpx]+2ln[(1−x/n)n−x(x/n)x]∼χ12​, two-sided, so too few exceptions is also a finding. Sixty paired days are needed before the page says anything.

Known limitations. One window, equally weighted (no filtered historical simulation yet); swaption and cap vol moves are in VaR through the ATM grid only, and cap vols have no P&L step (§11); the smile’s own moves enter the ladder VaR through vega × ATM only.

sections.title: Counterparty credit: netting sets and real-world exposure

blocks.html: Two measures

The same model is run under two parameter sets and every number is labelled with its measure. Risk-neutral: the Hull–White parameters of §9 calibrated to the swaption surface, each spot stepping with the ATM term structure of its pair’s surface (a desk default, labelled, for a pair without one), the drift from the curves; its outputs are the XVA reserves and belong to the P&L. Real-world: volatilities measured from two years of public history (daily changes of each currency’s 3M rate, log returns of each spot), a mean reversion set by policy (a=0.05; two years of daily data cannot identify it, and the estimate is shown beside it), zero drift by default (the forward slope is a risk-neutral artefact, the historical drift the firm’s alternative), and the correlation of all factor shocks from the same history; its outputs are EE, EPE, PFE and the limits.
Joint simulation

One Hull–White factor per currency and one lognormal factor per spot on a monthly grid to the netting set’s last maturity, Brownian motions correlated by the calibrated matrix (identity in the risk-neutral run). Grid times are each grid date’s distance from the as-of date in 365.25-day years, the clock every trade date is read on. The short rate is r(t)=f(0,t)+φ(t)+x(t) with x the driftless Ornstein–Uhlenbeck deviation and φ(t)=2a2σ2​(1−e−at)2; bonds are affine in x+φ and reproduce today’s curve,
P(t,T)=P(0,t)P(0,T)​exp(−B(t,T)(xt​+φ(t))−4aσ2​B(t,T)2(1−e−2at)),B(t,T)=a1−e−a(T−t)​.​(40)

(Until November 2026 the exponent was evaluated on xt​ alone, which priced every bond high by eBφ: 8bp at five years, 27bp at ten for a=3%, σ=85bp; the martingale check E[D(t)P(t,T)]=P(0,T) in the reference suite pins it.) Spots follow St​=S0​exp((μ−σ2/2)t+σWt​), μ the rate differential or zero. Historical sampling is the default real-world measure: each monthly step is a block of 21 consecutive observed daily changes from the calibration window, the block’s start drawn uniformly and the same block for every factor; the block’s sum is the step’s increment, in the Hull–White recursion xi​=xi−1​e−aΔt+∑Δr in place of σΔt​z, and the step’s log return for a spot; the panel is demeaned so the drift is the stated one. This keeps the window’s fat tails, its volatility clustering within a block and the realised co-movement of rates and spots without a correlation matrix; Gaussian shocks are the alternative, chosen per firm, and the fallback when a factor has no history on common dates.
Valuation on the paths, netting and the CSA

Every trade of a counterparty is valued on the same paths and summed per path and date, so netting is exact. A swap is valued from the path’s bonds: the fixed leg is ∑j​Ncτj​P(t,Tj​) over the coupons not yet paid, and the floating leg is the sum over its periods not yet paid, a period [s,e] paid at p≥e being worth
N(P(t,e)P(t,s)​−1)P(t,p)  (t<s),N(P(t,e)G(s,t)​−1)P(t,p)  (s≤t<e),N(G(s,e)−1)P(t,p)  (e≤t<p),(41)

where G(a,b) is what one unit placed at a has grown to by b on the path: the period’s interest accrued so far, with the unit. On the grid G is rolled at each step’s own bond, G(tk​,tk+1​)=1/P(tk​,tk+1​), and inside a step at the forward seen on the grid date before, so the discounted growth is a martingale and the rate’s variance inside one step is not in it; a span before the valuation date has no path behind it and grows at today’s rate for that length (the fixings are not read here). With p=e the first two are N(P(t,s)−P(t,e)) and N(G(s,t)−P(t,e)). The floating coupon is a cash flow of its step like a fixed one, the path’s own amount. Under a margin agreement the value a margin period back is drawn by a bridge between grid dates whose noise is the spread of the step’s change; in a step that holds a coupon that spread is the coupon’s and not the market’s, so the bridge is drawn on the value with its payments taken out and the payments made by each date are put back: a coupon is not a market move over the margin period. (Until version 1.32 the bridge was drawn on the value as it stood: at the last payment of a yearly swap, when nothing is left to move, the margined expected exposure stood at tens of thousands on ten million where it is now about nothing. The model validator, 17 November 2026; it held for fixed coupons as well.)

Until version 1.32 the whole leg was N(P(t,Ts​)−P(t,TN​)) with Ts​ read as t once the first period had begun, as if it reset at t, and TN​ the last payment date. The first left out the interest accrued since the period’s start: on a receive-fixed par swap with both legs yearly, worth nothing on average, the mean value stood at +34,628 a month into the year and +375,222 eleven months in on a notional of ten million at the par rate of a flat 4% curve (4.025%), and fell back at each payment. The second overvalued a leg that pays two days after each period ends, the ticket’s own swap, by about N(1−e−rδ) with δ the lag: 2,319 on ten million at the start of a five-year swap, less as its coupons are paid. The check that pins both does not use these formulas: the value at each grid date, discounted along the path, averages to today’s value of the coupons not yet paid at that date, read off today’s curve coupon by coupon; the discounting is done by the engine’s cash account and again by the trapezoid of the short rate, for yearly, half-yearly and quarterly floating legs, both directions, a two-day payment lag, a period ended and not yet paid, a swap begun ten days ago and one beginning in ten days, leverage and a spread, at every grid date, and to the dollar on the valuation date, where there is no sampling; and the accrual is compared path by path with the integrated short rate, since a mean cannot see the spread across paths that PFE is made of (tests/test\_ccr.py). The model validator derived the correction again with an account of the validator’s own (17 November 2026): the old value stood 53 to 1,800 standard errors from today’s curve between coupon dates, the new within 1.6. Where the two legs pay at different frequencies the saw-tooth that remains is real: three quarters of floating interest have been paid and the year’s fixed coupon has not. For a swap already running, the value at the start of the paths now carries the floating interest accrued to date: −201,000 on ten million for a yearly leg half a year in (the validator’s figure), where it carried the fixed leg’s accrual alone. Not done: that past part is at today’s rate, not from the fixings; no library reference for a swap’s value between coupon dates stands beside the martingale check. Forwards are valued as ±N(St​DFb​/DFq​−K)DFq​. Options are on the paths too: a cap’s or a floor’s period is Black’s formula on the growth of one unit over the period at the variance the paths’ own model gives it, then the realised payoff discounted to payment (§9, equations (10) and (11)); a cap, a floor and a collar are in the set since version 1.43, where they were listed as not simulated; a European swaption is Bachelier on the path’s forward swap rate at the normal vol the paths’ own Hull–White model implies for it (the Jamshidian price inverted through Bachelier, so value before expiry and exercise at expiry are one model and exposure does not step at expiry), then the underlying swap where it was in the money (physical settlement); an FX or digital-asset option is valued on the path’s forward at the surface’s forward vol for its remaining life and the smile at its moneyness (sticky-delta), its payoff fixed at the expiry grid point and discounted to settlement; barriers and touches carry which paths have knocked, monitored at the grid points seen so far; an American option is valued as its European. Anything else is listed as not simulated, never valued at zero. The CSA is the engine of §9: variation margin against the value lagged by the margin period of risk (a Brownian bridge inside the step), initial margin when the record says so, residual E+=max(V−C−IM,0).
Measures and limits

EE(t) the mean of E+; PFEq​(t) its q-quantile over paths at 95, 97.5 and 99%; EPE the time average of EE over the first year; the peak PFE95​ and its date; the largest PFE95​ in each tenor bucket; current exposure max(V0​−C0​,0). Credit limits are set on PFE_PEAK:<cpty>, PFE:<cpty>:<bucket>, EPE:<cpty>, CE:<cpty> and CVA:<cpty> with the same utilisation and breach rules as the market-risk limits. The reserves come from the risk-neutral paths through the waterfall of §9 with the counterparty’s spread (a desk default of 85bp and 40% LGD until the record carries its own).

Known limitations. The bridge noise is drawn independently per step, so the 99% tail is jagged month to month while the 95% profile is smooth; one factor per currency, so no curve twist in the exposure; the surface’s level does not move along a path (its term structure and smile are applied, §13; vol of vol is not simulated); the risk-neutral spot paths of a pair without a surface use a desk default vol, labelled; wrong-way risk and stressed EEPE are on the roadmap.

blocks.html: Collateral classes and the two CSAs

A CSA (§9) says whether collateral is exchanged; a regime says what it is and what each rulebook makes of it. A collateral class carries its recognition under the credit-risk-mitigation rules (CRE22.34–22.45; SCO60.94 for tokenised and crypto assets), its supervisory haircut by residual maturity (CRE22.49), its eligibility as initial and variation margin (CFTC §23.156), its liquidity level (LCR30) and its cryptoasset group (SCO60). A regime is a CSA, an eligible set, the compositions posted and received, and three labelled switches: close-out enforceability, the initial-margin eligibility state of a conditional class, and the margin period of risk (the non-cleared floor or the cleared floor for atomic settlement). From one regime the engine derives two CSAs:
regulatory:economic:​Creg​=C(1−h),h=1−∑i​wi​reci​(1−hi​),Ceco​=C when enforceable, else 0 (gross exposure),​(42)(43)​

with wi​ the composition weights, reci​∈{0,1} the recognition and hi​ the haircut; the regulatory reading is margined if and only if recognised variation margin is exchanged and enforceable. The regulatory CSA feeds SA-CCR, CVA capital and the leverage exposure; the economic CSA feeds CVA, DVA, FCA, FBA, MVA and ColVA, with the pickup on posted margin the yield of its eligible part. The all-recognised regime reproduces the plain CSA field by field, so every number of §9 is the cash-and-government-securities column.
Instruments, schedules and the carry over OIS

A class is a rulebook; an instrument is the asset: a code, its class, currency and issuer, its settlement rail (bilateral, or on chain with a token address), its yield source and an optional negotiated haircut. The yield source is a curve’s short rate plus a spread (cash in a currency on its OIS; government paper on the same curve until a government curve is loaded; a tokenised fund share at OIS less its expense ratio), a fixed rate the firm enters, or none (a payment stablecoin, a cryptoasset). The public seed is cash in three currencies, Treasury bills and notes, Bunds, Gilts, three payment stablecoins, a generic tokenised money-market fund share, a generic tokenised Treasury-bill claim and three cryptoassets; a firm adds its own instruments under its own names.

What the engines use is each instrument’s carry over OIS: a curve instrument on its currency’s OIS is its spread, a fixed rate is the rate less the OIS one-year zero of the account’s latest market, nothing is minus that OIS.

A schedule per counterparty (the credit support annex’s eligible-collateral list, versioned by effective date) names the admitted instruments, whether each is admitted for variation and for initial margin, a negotiated haircut and a concentration limit, the composition posted and received, and the rail. The regime of §16 is derived from it: the eligible classes are the instruments’ classes, the compositions aggregate by class, the on-chain rail sets the on-chain margin period, each class’s yield is the weighted carry of the instruments posted in it, and the two CSAs carry the weighted carries of the posted and received compositions, which ColVA integrates.

A cash schedule on the bilateral rail reproduces the class-level regime field by field (tests/test_collateral_instruments.py); on the ticket the trader may re-collateralise the same trade in any instrument on the firm’s list, and the on-chain comparison runs the same paths under atomic settlement with the chosen collateral, so the difference is the terms alone.

The cost difference between two regimes is quoted as a running spread over the trade’s annuity or an upfront spread of notional.
The book under regimes: attribution by channel

Every netting set is simulated once on the risk-neutral paths and re-collateralised step by step from the CSA as booked to an on-chain CSA under today’s rules (zero threshold and MTA, CRE52.18–52.19; daily margining, CRE52.50; the dispute doubling removed, CRE52.51; recognised collateral and enforceable netting, CRE22.34 and SCO60.94; eligible initial margin in the asset held at its yield, CFTC §23.156), then to the forward-looking states (the cleared-floor margin period of risk; a tokenised sovereign claim eligible as initial margin; Level 1 liquidity). Each step changes one thing in the previous step’s CSA and the difference it makes is that channel’s attribution, sequential as the P&L explain of §11; the steps sum to the columns exactly. The record’s margin period of risk is 9+N business days for re-margining every N days, floored at 10 and doubled while disputed. A record already on cash and government securities shows zero in the collateral step (parity, not superiority); the initial margin estimate moves only with the margin period of risk; market-risk capital is not a function of any step. Known limitations. Initial margin is the desk’s own amount or the engine’s estimate at the model’s current volatility (§9), not a regulatory margin model; supervisory deltas are held fixed along the path; the leverage and liquidity figures are the trade’s stock, not the ratios; a digital asset’s cryptoasset group is the engine’s default unless the desk sets it (§9).

blocks.html: The canonical record (schema v2, and v3 for an option on a rate)

Both parties sign one record that either can derive alone from its own booking. The record is keyed by the unique transaction identifier, names the two parties by LEI in sorted order, names the payer and receiver LEI of every leg, the buyer and seller of every embedded option and the payer and receiver of every custom cashflow, and orders legs by content. It contains only the economic terms: no internal references, no book or desk, no status, no timestamps, no party names. Serialisation rules, which a verifier in any language must reproduce exactly: JSON, UTF-8, keys sorted at every level, separators , and : with no whitespace; numbers as decimal strings without exponent, trailing zeros or negative zero; dates ISO-8601; nulls and booleans preserved; strings unchanged. The trade hash is h=keccak256(bytes). The schema version is inside the payload so a confirmation is always re-derived under the version it was signed with.

An option on a rate: schema v3 (since version 1.44). A swaption, a cap, a floor and a collar are signed under version 3, which is version 2 with one option block; every other product is signed under version 2 and its bytes are as they were. For a swaption the block names the buyer and the seller by LEI, the right (payer or receiver: what the buyer does with the fixed rate if it exercises), the exercise style, the expiry date, a Bermudan’s later exercise times as booked (in years from the trade date; none means the expiry date only), the strike, physical settlement, and the premium: its amount, currency and payment date. The legs are the swap delivered on exercise, with their own effective and termination dates, and each names the payer it will have if the buyer exercises: the buyer of a payer swaption pays the fixed rate, whichever side booked the trade. The trade block of a swaption holds no effective or maturity date: the option has its expiry and the swap its own dates. The strike is the fixed rate of the delivered swap as the leg holds it, to eight decimals; a booking whose two copies of it differ, one with no expiry, or one whose swap starts before the option expires, is refused a record. For a cap, a floor and a collar the strikes and the buyer and seller of each option were already on the leg (version 2); version 3 adds the premium, held unsigned with who pays it and who receives it (a collar whose floor is worth more than its cap pays the side that bought the cap). The buyer of a cap, a floor or a collar is read from the option on the leg (a collar’s from its cap), which the valuations read; a booking whose own side says otherwise, whose leg holds no such option, or whose collar has both options bought by one side, is refused a record. A booking with no premium has none in its record, and the paper confirmation says so: a premium is what the desk enters, never the model’s value in its place. A premium is a finite amount with a three-letter currency and a date; a swaption’s legs are booked as its holder’s swap (the fixed leg paid by the holder of a payer swaption) on both sides, and a booking whose legs say otherwise, or whose right is not stated, is refused.

Until version 1.44 a swaption was signed under version 2 as the swap it delivers and nothing else: the record held no buyer or seller, no expiry and no premium, the trade’s dates were the ticket’s (the swap’s as if it started at spot), and each leg’s payer was read from the ticket’s pay or receive choice, so a bought and a sold swaption were the same bytes and the sold one named the wrong payer. A confirmation signed under version 2 stays verifiable under version 2; its paper confirmation says what its record does not hold. The counterparty’s own booking of an option on a rate, made from the countersigned record, copied the booker’s side until this version, so both books held the same side of the option; it now holds the opposite one, and the two bookings derive the same version 3 record. Functions signing\_version, \_canonical\_v3; api/routes/trade\_cards.\_mirror\_option\_terms.
A package of trades confirmed as one

A package (a strip, a collar, a forward with an option) is several trades between the same two parties, booked together under one trade ID with a leg ID for each. Each leg keeps its own unique transaction identifier and its own canonical record, as above. What the parties sign and the registry anchors, once, is the package record: the schema name and version (rijeka-package, version 1), the two LEIs in sorted order and the keccak256 hashes of the legs’ records, sorted. It commits to every term of every leg, and each side derives the same bytes from its own bookings; neither firm’s reference for the package enters. A leg is proved by re-deriving its own record, finding its hash among the package’s legs, and re-deriving the package hash, which is the hash the signatures cover and the registry holds. The legs are confirmed together or not at all. One leg of a package cannot yet be amended or terminated on its own, since that is a new package record signed by both parties. Functions package_payload, package_hash; route /api/chain/confirm-package.
Signatures
Each party signs an EIP-712 typed message in the domain Rijeka Trade Confirmation, version 1, bound to the chain and the registry address:

Each party’s message names the other party’s address, so a signature cannot be replayed against a different counterparty, chain or registry. A firm’s signing address is registered in Rijeka through a wallet challenge; once registered, Rijeka can verify that firm’s signatures but can never produce them. On the hosted demo Rijeka holds keys for demo entities only, and any confirmation it signs for both sides is marked bilateral: false.
The registry

The registry contract has no owner and no administrative function. confirm verifies both signatures over the confirmation digest and records (h,partyA,partyB,timestamp) with status Confirmed; amend verifies both signatures over the amendment digest, marks the previous hash Superseded and records the new hash with the previous one as its parent; terminate verifies both signatures and sets Terminated. Signatures with high s values are rejected. Once a trade is anchored, Rijeka refuses off-chain edits to its terms: an amendment is itself a bilateral act.
Verification without Rijeka

A proof pack contains the canonical record, the hash, both signatures and the anchor. The public verifier, a single self-contained page, (i) re-serialises the record and recomputes the keccak256 hash, (ii) rebuilds both EIP-712 digests and recovers both signers, (iii) reads the registry on a public node and checks status and parties. No Rijeka server is contacted. The contract source is verified on Sourcify so the reader can audit what the registry does before trusting it. What it proves: that these exact terms were signed by these two keys and recorded at that block. What it does not prove: that a key belongs to a legal entity; that binding is a matter of the firms’ own key management and registration.
